stated_source: IT Act 2000, IT Amendment Act 2008, BNS 2023, DPDP Act 2023
text_to_review: Cyber law in India governs all crimes, offences, and legal issues arising from the use of computers, internet, mobile phones, and digital technology. The primary law is the Information Technology Act 2000 (IT Act) and its Amendment of 2008, along with relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) which replaced the IPC. The IT Act covers hacking, data theft, online fraud, cyberstalking, morphing, identity theft, phishing, ransomware, and publishing obscene content online. In 2023, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP Act) was also passed to protect citizens' personal data. In Uttar Pradesh, dedicated Cyber Crime cells operate in every district and the UP Police Cyber Crime department is headquartered in Lucknow. Cybercrime complaints can be filed online at cybercrime.gov.in or by calling the national cyber helpline 1930. UP Police also has a dedicated cyber complaint portal at upcop.gov.in. Cyber law applies to every citizen, company, and government body in India regardless of where the offender is located.

stated_source: MHA Cyber Crime Portal, UP Police, CERT-In, RBI
text_to_review: Where and how to report cybercrime in Uttar Pradesh? National Cyber Crime Helpline: 1930 — call immediately if you are a victim of online financial fraud; fastest way to freeze fraudulent transactions. Online portal: cybercrime.gov.in — file complaints for all types of cybercrime including financial fraud, cyber harassment, morphed images, sextortion, hacking, and child pornography. UP Police Cyber Crime portal: upcop.gov.in — for UP-specific complaints. Physical reporting: visit the Cyber Crime Cell of your district police or any police station and file an FIR or written complaint. For financial cyber fraud, also immediately call your bank to block the transaction and report to RBI at bankingombudsman.rbi.org.in. For social media account hacking or impersonation, also report directly to the platform — Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Google. For email fraud, report to CERT-In at incident@cert-in.org.in. Evidence to preserve before reporting: screenshots of the crime, URLs, chat logs, transaction IDs, email headers, and the fraudster's phone number or account details. Time is critical — report immediately, especially in financial fraud, as funds can be recovered if reported within hours.

stated_source: IT Act 2000 Section 66C, 66D, BNS 2023 Section 318, RBI Circular on Cyber Fraud
text_to_review: What is online financial fraud and what can victims do? Online financial fraud is the most common cybercrime in India and UP. Types include: UPI fraud — fraudster sends a collect request or tricks victim into scanning a QR code; OTP fraud — fraudster calls posing as bank or KYC officer and tricks victim into sharing OTP; phishing — fake websites or emails that steal banking credentials; SIM swap fraud — fraudster gets a duplicate SIM of victim's number and accesses bank accounts; investment fraud — fake apps or schemes promising high returns on investment; lottery and prize fraud — fraudulent messages claiming the victim has won a prize. What to do immediately: call 1930 within minutes; call your bank to freeze the account; file complaint at cybercrime.gov.in with transaction details. Legal provisions: online fraud is punishable under IT Act Section 66C (identity theft, up to 3 years), Section 66D (cheating by impersonation, up to 3 years), and BNS Section 318 (cheating). Victims can also approach the Banking Ombudsman for refund of fraudulently transferred funds. Courts have ordered banks to refund in several cases where the bank's security was at fault.

stated_source: IT Act 2000 Section 43, 66, 66B, BNS 2023
text_to_review: What is hacking and what are the legal provisions against it? Hacking means unauthorized access to any computer, server, mobile device, or network. Under IT Act Section 43 and Section 66, unauthorized access to a computer system is punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 5 lakh. Section 43 also covers unauthorized downloading of data, introducing viruses, damaging computer systems, and disrupting services. If hacking causes damage to a body corporate (company), compensation up to Rs 5 crore can be claimed. Data theft — stealing personal or business data from a computer — is covered under IT Act Section 43 and Section 66B (receiving stolen computer resource), punishable with up to 3 years. Ransomware attacks — where hackers encrypt data and demand payment — are punishable under IT Act Section 66 and BNS extortion provisions. Any business or individual whose computer system is hacked should: preserve evidence; file FIR at local police; report to CERT-In at cert-in.org.in which is India's nodal agency for cybersecurity incidents. In UP, the State Cyber Cell Lucknow handles major hacking cases.

stated_source: BNS 2023 Section 79, 351, IT Act Section 67, 66E
text_to_review: What is cyberstalking and online harassment and what legal action can be taken? Cyberstalking means using the internet, email, social media, or any electronic means to stalk, follow, monitor, or harass a person repeatedly causing fear or distress. Online harassment includes sending threatening or abusive messages, creating fake profiles to defame someone, sending unsolicited sexual content, and doxxing (publishing someone's private information online). Legal provisions: BNS Section 79 (stalking including cyberstalking) — up to 3 years for first offence, up to 5 years for repeat; IT Act Section 67 (publishing obscene material online) — up to 3 years and Rs 5 lakh fine; BNS Section 351 (criminal intimidation by sending threatening messages) — up to 7 years. For women victims, additional provisions under BNS Section 75 apply. What to do: preserve all evidence including screenshots and message records; block the harasser on the platform; report the profile to the social media platform; file complaint at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930; file FIR at nearest police station or Cyber Crime Cell. In UP, women can also call 1090 for cyberstalking complaints.

stated_source: IT Act 2000 Section 66E, 67A, BNS 2023 Section 79, CCPWC Portal
text_to_review: What is image morphing and sextortion and what legal protections exist? Morphing means digitally altering someone's photos to make them obscene or defamatory and sharing them online. Sextortion means threatening to share intimate or morphed images unless the victim pays money or complies with demands. Both are serious crimes. Legal provisions: IT Act Section 66E — violation of privacy by capturing, publishing, or transmitting private images without consent, punishable with up to 3 years and Rs 2 lakh fine; IT Act Section 67A — publishing sexually explicit material electronically, punishable with up to 5 years and Rs 10 lakh fine; BNS Section 79 — cyberstalking including persistent online contact. What victims should do: do not pay the sextortionist as it encourages further demands; preserve all evidence; immediately report at cybercrime.gov.in selecting the Women and Children category; call 1930 or 1090 (for women in UP); request the platform to take down the content; file FIR with Cyber Crime Cell. Platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and Google have takedown mechanisms for non-consensual intimate images. Courts in India have granted emergency interim relief to victims including immediate takedown orders.

stated_source: BNS 2023 Section 356, 197, 353, IT Act Section 66C, 66D
text_to_review: What are the laws on social media defamation, fake news, and impersonation? Defamation online — posting false statements of fact that damage someone's reputation — is covered under BNS Section 356 (defamation), punishable with up to 2 years imprisonment. Creating a fake profile in someone's name to defame, cheat, or harass them is covered under IT Act Section 66C (identity theft, up to 3 years) and IT Act Section 66D (cheating by impersonation, up to 3 years). Spreading fake news or misinformation that causes public panic, communal tension, or harm to national integrity is covered under BNS Section 197 and 353. What victims can do: gather screenshot evidence; report the fake profile directly to the social media platform for removal; file FIR at Cyber Crime Cell or nearest police station; file complaint at cybercrime.gov.in. For urgent cases, approach the High Court for an emergency injunction to remove defamatory content. Government officials or public servants posting inflammatory content can also face action under service rules. In UP, spreading communally sensitive misinformation online is taken very seriously by UP Police and frequently results in arrests.

stated_source: POCSO Act 2012 Section 13-15, IT Act Section 67B, BNS 2023
text_to_review: What are the laws protecting children from online abuse and exploitation? Children face serious online threats including grooming, cyberbullying, exposure to pornographic content, and online sexual exploitation. Legal provisions: POCSO Act 2012 Section 13-15 — using a child for pornographic content or storing child sexual abuse material (CSAM) carries 5 to 7 years imprisonment; IT Act Section 67B — publishing or transmitting material depicting children in sexually explicit acts carries up to 7 years imprisonment; BNS Section 74 — assault or sexual harassment of a child. Platforms are legally required to report child sexual abuse material to NCMEC and Indian authorities. Parents and guardians must report: visit cybercrime.gov.in and select the Child Pornography or Child Sexual Abuse Material category; call 1098 Childline for children in immediate danger; report to NCPCR at ncpcr.gov.in. Schools in UP are mandated under POCSO to have a child protection policy and designated teacher for reporting. Cyberbullying of children should be reported to school authorities, the platform, and Cyber Crime Cell. Identity of child victims is fully protected by law.

stated_source: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, IT Act Section 43A, CERT-In
text_to_review: What are citizens' rights regarding personal data privacy under Indian law? The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (DPDP Act) is India's landmark data privacy law. Key rights of every citizen (called Data Principal): Right to information — you can ask any company or government body (called Data Fiduciary) what personal data they hold about you; Right to correction — you can demand correction of inaccurate personal data; Right to erasure — you can request deletion of your personal data when it is no longer necessary; Right to grievance redressal — every Data Fiduciary must have a grievance officer; Right to nominate — you can nominate someone to exercise your rights in case of death or incapacity. Data Fiduciaries must: obtain free, informed, and specific consent before processing personal data; use data only for the stated purpose; protect data with reasonable security measures; report data breaches to the Data Protection Board within prescribed time. The Data Protection Board of India will adjudicate complaints. Currently citizens can file data privacy complaints with CERT-In or approach consumer forums. For Aadhaar data misuse, contact UIDAI at 1947 or grievances.uidai.gov.in.

stated_source: IT Act 2000 Section 66C, 66D, BNS 2023 Section 318, CERT-In Advisories
text_to_review: What are phishing and email scams and how can people protect themselves and seek remedy? Phishing means fraudulent emails, SMS, or WhatsApp messages that appear to come from trusted sources like banks, UIDAI, IT department, or courts, tricking victims into revealing passwords, OTPs, or personal information. Common scams targeting UP residents: fake KYC update messages threatening to block bank account or SIM; fake income tax refund emails asking for bank details; fake job offer emails asking for registration fees; fake lottery win messages; courier fraud calls claiming a parcel has illegal items. Legal provisions: IT Act Section 66C (identity theft) and Section 66D (cheating by impersonation) — both punishable with up to 3 years; BNS Section 318 (cheating). Prevention tips: never share OTP with anyone on call; no bank ever asks for your password; verify by calling the official number; check sender email address carefully for slight spelling differences. If victimized: call 1930 immediately; file complaint at cybercrime.gov.in; inform your bank; preserve all messages as evidence. CERT-In regularly publishes advisories about active phishing campaigns at cert-in.org.in.

stated_source: Information Technology Act 2000, IT Amendment Act 2008
text_to_review: What are the key sections of the IT Act 2000 that every citizen should know? Section 43: Penalty for unauthorized access to computer — compensation up to Rs 1 crore. Section 65: Tampering with computer source code — up to 3 years and Rs 2 lakh fine. Section 66: Computer related offences (hacking) — up to 3 years and Rs 5 lakh fine. Section 66A: (Struck down by Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal case 2015) — was used to arrest people for social media posts. Section 66B: Receiving stolen computer resource — up to 3 years. Section 66C: Identity theft — up to 3 years and Rs 1 lakh fine. Section 66D: Cheating by personation using computer — up to 3 years and Rs 1 lakh fine. Section 66E: Violation of privacy — up to 3 years and Rs 2 lakh fine. Section 66F: Cyber terrorism — up to life imprisonment. Section 67: Publishing obscene material online — up to 3 years. Section 67A: Publishing sexually explicit material — up to 5 years. Section 67B: Child pornography — up to 7 years. Section 69: Government power to intercept or monitor information — with safeguards. Section 72: Breach of confidentiality and privacy by officials — up to 2 years.

stated_source: IT Act 2000 Section 66F, National Cyber Security Policy
text_to_review: What is cyber terrorism and what are the legal provisions? Cyber terrorism under IT Act Section 66F means using computers or internet to threaten the unity, integrity, security, or sovereignty of India, or to strike terror in people by denying access to computer resources, or by penetrating critical infrastructure. This includes attacks on power grids, banking systems, defence systems, and communication networks. Punishment for cyber terrorism is life imprisonment. It is one of the most serious offences under Indian cyber law. Threats to bomb or attack critical infrastructure sent via email or social media are also covered. In practice, cyber terrorism provisions are invoked for: attacks on government websites; spreading content that incites communal violence; coordinated disinformation campaigns targeting national security. Cyber terrorism complaints go to the National Investigation Agency (NIA) and the National Cyber Security Coordinator under the Prime Minister's Office. CERT-In is the nodal agency for protecting critical information infrastructure. Citizens who come across content threatening national security online should report at cybercrime.gov.in and to their local police.

stated_source: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023, Section 57-63, IT Act 2000 Section 79A
text_to_review: How is digital evidence collected and used in cyber crime cases? Digital evidence includes emails, chat messages, social media posts, call records, CCTV footage, GPS location data, browser history, transaction records, and any data stored on electronic devices. Under the Indian Evidence Act (now Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023), electronic records are admissible as evidence if they meet certain conditions: the computer or device was used regularly and working properly; the data was stored or transmitted in the ordinary course of activities; the device was operating properly at the time. A certificate under Section 63 of Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam from the person responsible for the device must be provided for electronic evidence. Key tips for victims: take screenshots with date and time visible; do not delete any messages or records even if they are disturbing; note down URLs, profile links, and phone numbers; if possible get the evidence certified by a notary. Police cyber cells have forensic tools to recover deleted data from devices. Courts regularly accept WhatsApp screenshots, call records, email printouts, and transaction history as evidence in cyber crime cases.

stated_source: IT (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules 2021, Constitution Article 19, Supreme Court Shreya Singhal judgment 2015
text_to_review: What are citizens' rights and limits on social media in India? Every citizen has the right to free speech and expression online under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution — but this right has reasonable restrictions. What is allowed: sharing opinions, political commentary, criticism of government policies, satire, and factual reporting. What is NOT allowed and can lead to criminal action: posting content that threatens national security or sovereignty; spreading content that promotes enmity between communities or religions; posting obscene or sexually explicit content; making false statements that damage someone's reputation (defamation); sharing someone's private images without consent; posting content that incites violence. The IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021 require large social media platforms to appoint a Grievance Officer in India. Every platform must resolve user complaints within 15 days. Users can report content to the platform and also escalate to the Grievance Appellate Committee set up by the government if the platform does not act. Citizens wrongly arrested for social media posts should know that IT Act Section 66A was struck down by the Supreme Court and cannot be applied.

stated_source: Aadhaar Act 2016, UIDAI Regulations, IT Act 2000
text_to_review: What are the laws protecting Aadhaar data and what to do if it is misused? Aadhaar is protected under the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act 2016. Key protections: no one can compel you to share your Aadhaar biometrics for authentication except for government schemes; sharing or misusing Aadhaar data without authorization is punishable with up to 3 years imprisonment and Rs 10 lakh fine; impersonating someone using their Aadhaar carries up to 3 years. Aadhaar number sharing should be limited — use a masked Aadhaar (which shows only the last 4 digits) for non-essential purposes. If your Aadhaar is misused or linked to a mobile number or bank account without your consent: lock your Aadhaar biometrics at myaadhaar.uidai.gov.in or call UIDAI helpline 1947; check which mobile numbers are linked to your Aadhaar at tafcop.dgtelecom.gov.in; report unauthorized linking to UIDAI at grievances.uidai.gov.in; file cybercrime complaint at cybercrime.gov.in. Never share your Aadhaar OTP with anyone. Fake UIDAI update calls and messages are a common phishing scam in UP — always verify by calling 1947 directly.

stated_source: IT Act 2000 Section 79, IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021
text_to_review: What is intermediary liability and are platforms like WhatsApp and Facebook responsible for content? Under IT Act Section 79, intermediaries like WhatsApp, Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and Twitter are not liable for third-party content if they act as a neutral conduit and follow due diligence rules. However, platforms lose this safe harbour protection if they have actual knowledge of illegal content and fail to take it down promptly. The IT (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules 2021 require significant social media platforms (with more than 50 lakh users) to: appoint a Chief Compliance Officer, Nodal Contact Person, and Grievance Officer in India; acknowledge user complaints within 24 hours and resolve within 15 days; proactively identify and remove child sexual abuse material; trace the first originator of a message when required by government order (relevant for WhatsApp). Users who are aggrieved by platform decisions can approach the Grievance Appellate Committee. Platforms that repeatedly fail to act on court orders or government notices can be made liable for hosted content. This means victims of defamation or harassment can sue both the poster and the platform in some circumstances.

stated_source: UP Police Cyber Cell, MHA Cyber Crime Portal, UP STF
text_to_review: How does UP Police investigate cybercrime cases? Uttar Pradesh has a dedicated Cyber Crime investigation infrastructure. The UP Cyber Crime department is headquartered in Lucknow with district-level Cyber Crime Cells in all 75 districts. When a cybercrime complaint is filed: if filed online at cybercrime.gov.in, it is assigned to the relevant state or district cyber cell; if filed at a local police station, it is forwarded to the district Cyber Crime Cell for investigation; in financial fraud cases, the 1930 helpline coordinates between banks, payment gateways, and police to freeze fraudulent accounts. UP Police Cyber Cell has tools for: IP address tracing; social media account identification; call detail record (CDR) analysis; device forensics. For major cases involving organized cybercrime gangs, the UP STF (Special Task Force) Cyber Cell Lucknow leads investigation. Cooperation with international agencies like Interpol and CBI Cyber Division is sought for cross-border cybercrimes. Victims should always get a written acknowledgment of their complaint and follow up with the concerned Cyber Cell. Complaints can be tracked at cybercrime.gov.in using the complaint number.

stated_source: DPDP Act 2023, Puttaswamy judgment 2017, IT (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules 2021
text_to_review: What is the right to be forgotten and can people get content removed from the internet? The right to be forgotten — the right to have personal information removed from the internet — is an emerging right in India. The Supreme Court in the Puttaswamy judgment 2017 recognized the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21, which forms the basis for right to be forgotten. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 includes a right to erasure of personal data. In practice, individuals can: request removal of personal data from company databases under DPDP Act; approach High Courts for removal of private information published without consent; request search engines like Google to de-index harmful or outdated content through their removal request tools; approach the IT Grievance Appellate Committee if platforms refuse to remove content; for court order related information, approach the concerned court to restrict public access. Sensitive categories of information such as medical records, sexual orientation, and financial details have stronger protection. Victims of revenge porn, defamation, or unauthorized data publishing have successfully obtained court orders for content removal in India including from UP High Court at Allahabad.

stated_source: IT Act Section 43A, CERT-In Directions 2022, DPDP Act 2023
text_to_review: What cyber law compliance obligations do businesses in UP have? Businesses that handle personal data or operate digital systems have significant obligations under Indian cyber law. Key compliance requirements: IT Act Section 43A — body corporates that possess, deal with, or handle sensitive personal data must implement reasonable security practices; failure causing wrongful loss can lead to compensation liability. CERT-In Directions 2022 — all service providers, intermediaries, data centres, and body corporates must: report cybersecurity incidents to CERT-In within 6 hours; maintain logs of all IT systems for 180 days; mandatorily use NTP servers for time synchronization. DPDP Act 2023 — businesses must obtain valid consent before processing personal data; appoint a Data Protection Officer if processing large volumes; implement data security measures. E-commerce businesses must comply with Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020. Fintech businesses must follow RBI cybersecurity guidelines. Penalty for non-compliance: CERT-In can impose penalties; DPDP Act allows fines up to Rs 250 crore per violation. Small businesses in UP can contact UP MSME department or STPI Lucknow for guidance on cyber compliance.

stated_source: IT Act 2000, BNS 2023, CERT-In, UP Police Cyber Cell, MHA Cyber Crime Portal
text_to_review: Common real life cyber law situations in UP and where to go. Money transferred to fraud UPI account: call 1930 immediately, call bank to freeze account, file complaint at cybercrime.gov.in with transaction ID. Fake job offer asking for registration fees: file complaint at cybercrime.gov.in, report the phone number to DoT at sancharsaathi.gov.in. Morphed photos shared on WhatsApp groups: report to platform for takedown, file complaint at cybercrime.gov.in selecting Women and Children category, call 1090 for women victims. Social media account hacked: report to platform immediately, change all linked passwords, file complaint at cybercrime.gov.in, file FIR at Cyber Crime Cell. Someone creating fake Facebook or Instagram profile in your name: report to platform, file complaint at cybercrime.gov.in under cyber impersonation, file FIR under IT Act Section 66C and 66D. Aadhaar linked to unknown mobile number without consent: lock Aadhaar biometrics at myaadhaar.uidai.gov.in, call UIDAI at 1947, file complaint. Receiving threats or abusive messages online: preserve screenshots, file FIR at nearest police station or Cyber Crime Cell, apply for protection order from Magistrate. Business website hacked: report to CERT-In at cert-in.org.in, file FIR with UP Cyber Crime Cell, restore from backup.

stated_source: Family Courts Act 1984, Hindu Marriage Act 1955, Muslim Personal Law, Special Marriage Act 1954
text_to_review: Family law in India governs personal matters like marriage, divorce, maintenance, child custody, adoption, guardianship, and inheritance. India has a plural legal system where different personal laws apply based on religion: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 and Hindu Succession Act 1956 for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs; Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937 for Muslims; Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872 and Divorce Act 1869 for Christians; Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936 for Parsis. The Special Marriage Act 1954 applies to inter-religion marriages and civil marriages. In Uttar Pradesh, family disputes are heard by Family Courts in every district under the Family Courts Act 1984. Family Courts have exclusive jurisdiction over matrimonial disputes, maintenance, custody, and guardianship. Free legal aid is available from the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) in every UP district for women, children, and economically weaker persons. Mediation is strongly encouraged in Family Courts before litigation begins. The Allahabad High Court supervises all Family Courts in UP and has passed several landmark judgments on maintenance and custody.

stated_source: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 Section 8, igrsup.gov.in, Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006
text_to_review: What are the rules for marriage registration in UP? Marriage registration provides legal proof for passport, visa, property, and insurance purposes. In UP, Hindu marriages are registered under the Hindu Marriage Act 1955 through the online portal igrsup.gov.in run by the UP Registration and Stamp Department. Process: both spouses apply online at igrsup.gov.in; attend the Sub-Registrar's office of the area; submit marriage certificate from priest or temple, wedding photographs, age proof (Aadhaar, birth certificate), address proof, and two witnesses with ID; certificate is issued after verification. Fee is nominal. Muslim marriages are registered through the Waqf Board or local Qazi — registration is not mandatory under Muslim personal law but strongly advisable. Christian marriages are registered at the church and under the Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872. Civil marriages under Special Marriage Act 1954 are registered with the Marriage Officer (Sub-Registrar) of the district. Minimum age: 18 years for women and 21 years for men — marrying below this age is illegal under Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006. UP government has integrated marriage registration with Aadhaar for authenticity.

stated_source: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 Section 13, 13B, Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019, Divorce Act 1869
text_to_review: What are the grounds and process for divorce in UP? Divorce law varies by religion. For Hindus under Hindu Marriage Act 1955, grounds for divorce include: cruelty, adultery, desertion for 2 or more years, conversion to another religion, mental disorder, leprosy, venereal disease, renunciation of world, and presumption of death. Mutual consent divorce: both parties can file for divorce by mutual consent under Section 13B HMA; after 6 months cooling off period (courts can waive this under Supreme Court ruling), divorce is granted. For Muslims: instant triple talaq is banned under Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019 — punishable with 3 years imprisonment; a Muslim woman can seek divorce through Khula or court-based Faskh. For Christians: Divorce Act 1869 applies — grounds include adultery, conversion, insanity, and cruelty. Special Marriage Act: divorce grounds similar to Hindu Marriage Act. All divorce petitions in UP are filed at the Family Court of the district where the couple last lived together. Filing fee is nominal. Average time for contested divorce in UP Family Courts is 2 to 5 years; mutual consent divorce typically takes 6 to 18 months. Free legal aid is available from DLSA for women in divorce cases.

stated_source: BNSS 2023 Section 144, Hindu Marriage Act 1955 Section 24-25, Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986
text_to_review: What is maintenance and who can claim it in UP? Maintenance means financial support ordered by a court for the upkeep of a spouse, children, or parents. Section 144 of BNSS 2023 (earlier Section 125 CrPC) provides a secular remedy for all religions: a wife, minor children, and parents who cannot maintain themselves can claim maintenance from the husband or adult son. Who can claim: wife including divorced wife until remarriage; minor children including illegitimate children; adult children with physical or mental disability; parents who cannot maintain themselves. Amount: the court decides based on the claimant's needs and the payer's income — there is no fixed minimum or maximum. Interim maintenance can be ordered quickly within weeks while the main case is pending. Non-payment of maintenance order is punishable with 1 month imprisonment. In addition to Section 144 BNSS, Hindu wives can claim maintenance under Section 24 and 25 of Hindu Marriage Act. Muslim divorced women are entitled to maintenance under Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986 and the Supreme Court's landmark Mohd Ahmed Khan vs Shah Bano Begum judgment. In UP, maintenance applications are filed at the Family Court of the district. DLSA provides free legal aid for maintenance cases.

stated_source: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956, Guardian and Wards Act 1890, Family Courts Act 1984
text_to_review: What are the rules for child custody after separation or divorce in UP? Child custody is decided by the Family Court based on the best interests of the child — this is the paramount consideration above all else including parental rights. Types of custody: Physical custody — child lives with one parent; Legal custody — right to make decisions about child's education, health, and welfare (can be joint); Sole custody — one parent has both; Joint custody — both parents share. Factors considered: age of child (children below 5 usually with mother); financial stability of each parent; emotional bonding; educational needs; child's own preference for older children. Interim custody can be granted quickly while the main case is pending. Visitation rights are usually given to the non-custodial parent — typically alternate weekends and holidays. Taking the child to another city or country without court permission is contempt of court and can amount to kidnapping under BNS. In UP, custody matters go to the Family Court of the district. For NRI custody cases, the Allahabad High Court has specific guidelines under the Hague Convention framework. Grandparents can apply for visitation rights under Guardian and Wards Act 1890. Mediation through the Family Court counsellor is strongly encouraged for custody arrangements.

stated_source: BNS 2023 Section 85, 303, 316, PWDVA 2005, Allahabad High Court judgments on streedhan
text_to_review: What is streedhan and what are a woman's rights over her gifts and jewelry in UP? Streedhan is all property — cash, jewelry, gifts, and assets — given to a woman before, during, or after marriage by her parents, in-laws, husband, or relatives. Streedhan is the absolute and exclusive property of the woman — no one else has any right over it. The husband or in-laws cannot demand, take, or use streedhan without the woman's consent. Taking or withholding streedhan is a criminal offence under Section 85 BNS (cruelty) and also amounts to theft or criminal breach of trust under BNS. A woman leaving her matrimonial home due to cruelty or divorce has the right to recover all her streedhan regardless of how long ago it was taken. If streedhan is withheld, the woman can: file FIR at Mahila Thana or nearest police station; approach the Family Court for recovery order; file complaint under PWDVA 2005 for monetary relief to recover streedhan. The Allahabad High Court has in several judgments upheld women's right to recover streedhan even years after separation. In UP, the Mahila Thana in each district handles streedhan complaints. The UP State Women Commission also intervenes in streedhan recovery cases when police are unresponsive.

stated_source: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005, Section 12, 17, 18, 19, 20, 22
text_to_review: What family law remedies are available for domestic violence victims in UP? The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 (PWDVA) provides civil remedies for women facing domestic violence. Domestic violence under PWDVA includes physical violence, sexual violence by husband, emotional and verbal abuse, and economic abuse such as denying household expenses or taking away streedhan. Remedies: Protection Order — restrains abuser from committing acts of violence; Residence Order — wife cannot be thrown out of shared household even if it belongs to in-laws; Monetary Relief — for medical expenses, loss of earnings, maintenance, and streedhan recovery; Custody Order — temporary custody of children; Compensation Order — for injuries and mental agony. How to file in UP: approach the Protection Officer at the District Social Welfare Office of your district; or file application directly before the Judicial Magistrate First Class of the district; or approach any NGO recognized as a Service Provider under PWDVA. In UP, Protection Officers are appointed in all 75 districts. The Magistrate must hear the matter within 3 days of filing. Emergency protection orders can be issued the same day in urgent situations. Call 1090 Women Helpline or 112 for immediate police assistance. Free legal aid is available from DLSA.

stated_source: Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006, BNS 2023, UP Mission Shakti
text_to_review: What is the law against child marriage in UP and how to report it? Child marriage is prohibited under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 (PCMA). Minimum age for marriage is 18 years for girls and 21 years for boys. A child marriage is voidable at the option of the minor — the child can get it declared void by approaching the court within 2 years of becoming an adult. Under BNS, a girl married below 18 can seek annulment at any time. Punishment: anyone who solemnizes, conducts, directs, or permits child marriage including parents, guardians, priests, and relatives can be imprisoned for up to 2 years and fined Rs 1 lakh. Every district in UP has a Child Marriage Prohibition Officer (CMPO) — usually the District Probation Officer. How to report in UP: call Childline 1098; call 112 UP Police; report to the CMPO of the district; approach the Child Welfare Committee; file complaint at the nearest police station. text_to_review:
What is an FIR and when should you file one?

FIR stands for First Information Report. It is the first official complaint registered with the police when a cognizable offence occurs. Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023 — which replaced the old CrPC from July 1, 2024 — FIR is governed by Section 173 (formerly CrPC Section 154).

A cognizable offence is a crime where police can arrest a person without a court warrant — such as murder, rape, kidnapping, dacoity, robbery, and theft above Rs. 5,000. For these crimes, registering an FIR is mandatory — police have no legal right to refuse.

A non-cognizable offence is a minor crime like petty verbal abuse or a small scuffle — for these, police register an NCR (Non-Cognizable Report) instead, and need a Magistrate's order before they can investigate.

You should file an FIR immediately when: you are a victim of a serious crime, you have witnessed a cognizable offence, or you have reliable information about such an offence.

In Uttar Pradesh, you can: visit any police station, call UP 112 (24x7 emergency), call 1090 (for women), file online at uppolice.gov.in, or approach a Judicial Magistrate directly if police refuse.

There is no time limit to file an FIR — you can file it months or even years after a crime. However, filing promptly is strongly advised because evidence degrades over time, witnesses forget details, and medical injuries heal. The sooner you file, the stronger your case.

Key law: BNSS Section 173 (formerly CrPC 154). Both section references are currently in use since the law recently changed.

stated_source: BNSS Sections 35, 47, 58, 173, 175; Constitution Article 22; BNS Section 202
text_to_review:
Your legal rights when filing an FIR — what police must do and cannot deny

Every citizen in India has strong legal rights related to FIR. These rights come from the BNSS 2023, the Constitution of India, and Supreme Court judgments.

1. Right to FIR registration: Police CANNOT refuse to register an FIR for a cognizable offence. Refusal is itself a punishable crime under BNS Section 202 (formerly IPC 166A) — the officer can face 6 months to 2 years imprisonment.

2. Right to a free FIR copy: Immediately after registration, you are entitled to a free copy of the FIR. The copy must carry the FIR number, station seal, and officer's signature.

3. Right to file FIR in your language: You can give information in Hindi or your local language. English is not required. If you cannot write, the officer must write it for you — BNSS Section 173(1).

4. Right to a woman officer for women's crimes: For offences like rape, sexual assault, and crimes under BNS Sections 64–73, the FIR MUST be recorded by a woman police officer — BNSS Section 173(1) proviso.

5. Zero FIR right: You can file an FIR at ANY police station regardless of jurisdiction. The station must transfer it to the correct area police station afterward.

6. Right to escalate SP: If police refuse, you can give written information to the SP — BNSS Section 173(3). The SP must either investigate or order investigation.

7. Magistrate remedy: You can approach a Judicial Magistrate under BNSS Section 175(3) who can order police to investigate and register FIR.

8. New BNSS 2023 rights on arrest: Police must prepare an arrest memo (Section 35). You have the right to inform one person of your arrest (Section 35(3)). You must be produced before Magistrate within 24 hours (Section 58).

9. Right to free legal aid: If you cannot afford a lawyer, NALSA (15100) and UP State Legal Services Authority (0522-2209457) provide free legal representation.

stated_source: BNSS Section 173, 175, 176; uppolice.gov.in
text_to_review:
Step-by-step process to file an FIR in Uttar Pradesh

Step 1 — Visit the police station: Go to the nearest police station or the station covering the area where the crime occurred. Ask to meet the SHO (Station House Officer) or the duty officer in charge. You have the right to file at any time — police stations are open 24 hours.

Step 2 — Report the crime: Give the officer all details — date, time, location, what happened, who did it, how many people were involved, what was stolen or damaged, and any injuries. Speak in Hindi or your language. The officer is required to write it down if you cannot write (BNSS Section 173(1)).

Step 3 — Verify and sign: The officer will read back what was written. Verify every detail before signing or giving your thumb impression. Do not sign if anything is missing or incorrect — ask for corrections first.

Step 4 — Collect your FIR copy: Immediately ask for your free copy of the FIR. Note the FIR number. Take a photograph of the copy as a backup. The copy is your proof that the FIR was registered.

Step 5 — If police refuses: (a) Ask for refusal in writing. (b) File written complaint to SP under BNSS 173(3). (c) File online at uppolice.gov.in. (d) Call 112 or 1090 (women). (e) Approach Judicial Magistrate under BNSS 175(3).

Step 6 — After filing: Track your FIR status at uppolice.gov.in. Keep all documents — FIR copy, medical reports, photographs, and witness contact information. If investigation is not progressing, approach SP or the Magistrate.

Practical tips: Take a witness to the police station. If you have injuries, get a medical certificate (MLC — Medico-Legal Certificate) from a doctor before or immediately after filing FIR. Do not alter or destroy any evidence. Do not post on social media before or during investigation as it can compromise the case.

Time limits and deadlines in FIR and police complaint process

For Filing an FIR:
There is no statutory deadline to file an FIR. You can report a crime months or years after it happened. Courts have accepted delayed FIRs in genuine cases. However, unexplained long delays may reduce the credibility of your complaint in court. File as early as possible.

For Police After Arrest:
24 hours — Police must produce any arrested person before a Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest. This is mandatory under BNSS Section 58 (formerly CrPC 57). Exceeding this without Magistrate's order is illegal detention.

For Chargesheet Filing:
60 days — Standard cognizable cases: Police must file chargesheet (police report under BNSS Section 193) within 60 days of the accused's arrest.
90 days — Serious cases: For offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or 10+ years, the deadline is 90 days.

Consequence of missing these deadlines: If police fail to file within 60 or 90 days respectively, and the accused is still in custody, the accused gets the right to Default Bail (also called Statutory Bail) under BNSS Section 187(2). This bail is a right — the Magistrate must grant it. Important: the accused must apply for Default Bail BEFORE the chargesheet is filed. Once chargesheet is filed — even if delayed — this right expires.

For Bail Applications:
Anticipatory bail — No time limit. Apply the moment you fear arrest.
Regular bail — No time limit after arrest, but apply quickly to avoid long custody.

For SP Complaint: File immediately after refusal — within 24–48 hours ideally.
For Magistrate Application (BNSS 175(3)): File as soon as SP complaint fails — no fixed limit but delay weakens the case.
For High Court FIR quashing petition: No fixed limit, but courts prefer timely petitions.

Penalties — for police misconduct and for filing false complaints

Police Are Not Above the Law — Penalties for Police Misconduct:

1. Refusing to register FIR for cognizable offence: Under BNS Section 202 (formerly IPC 166A), a police officer who refuses to register an FIR or fails to record information as required can face 6 months to 2 years imprisonment and a fine. This is a serious criminal offence.

2. Failure to investigate after FIR: If a police officer deliberately neglects to investigate a cognizable offence after FIR registration — same penalty applies under BNS 202.

3. Custodial torture: If police beat or torture a person in custody to extract a confession — BNS Section 117 (formerly IPC 330) applies. Punishment: up to 7 years imprisonment and fine. Victims can also file a complaint with the State Human Rights Commission or NHRC.

4. Illegal detention: Detaining a person beyond 24 hours without Magistrate's order — BNS Section 132 (formerly IPC 342). Punishment: 1 year imprisonment or Rs. 5,000 fine or both.

5. Destroying evidence: If anyone — including a police officer — conceals, destroys, or tampers with evidence — BNS Section 238 (formerly IPC 201). Punishment: up to 7 years depending on the severity of the underlying offence.

6. Threatening witnesses: Inducing or threatening a witness to give false evidence or stay silent — BNS Section 227 (formerly IPC 195A). Punishment: up to 7 years imprisonment.

Penalty for False FIR:
Filing a false FIR against an innocent person is a criminal offence under BNS Section 215 (formerly IPC 182). Punishment: 6 months imprisonment or fine or both. This applies to citizens — not just police. Always provide truthful, accurate information in an FIR.

How to Complain Against Police Misconduct in UP:
- SP's office — written complaint
- CM Helpline: 1076
- UP Anti-Corruption Helpline: 1064
- UP Human Rights Commission — Lucknow
- National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) — New Delhi

text_to_review:
What to do when police refuse to act — escalation levels in Uttar Pradesh

If police are not registering your FIR or not investigating — here is your complete escalation roadmap, from easiest to strongest:

Level 1 — SHO at the Police Station:
Start here. Ask to meet the Station House Officer (SHO) in person. Present your complaint clearly. Request the FIR to be registered. Ask for a written acknowledgement of your visit.

Level 2 — SP / DSP Office (BNSS Section 173(3)):
If SHO refuses, go to the District Superintendent of Police (SP) or Deputy SP (DSP) office. Submit a written complaint under BNSS Section 173(3). The SP has authority to order the station to register the FIR or investigate directly. Get an acknowledgement slip.

Level 3 — UP Police Online Portal and CM Helpline:
File an online complaint at uppolice.gov.in. Call CM Helpline 1076 — this directly logs a complaint that is tracked and followed up by a state-level team. This is particularly effective in UP.

Level 4 — Judicial Magistrate (BNSS Section 175(3)):
This is the strongest non-court remedy. File a written application before the Judicial Magistrate of your district. The Magistrate can directly ORDER police to register FIR and investigate. Court fee is minimal (Rs. 10–50). You do not need a lawyer, though one is helpful. Attach proof of your SP complaint.

Level 5 — UP High Court (BNSS Section 528 / old CrPC 482):
If all else fails, file a petition in UP High Court Allahabad. The High Court can: order police to investigate, quash a false FIR filed against you, or take action against errant police officers. This requires a lawyer.

Level 6 — Human Rights Commissions:
For cases involving police brutality, illegal detention, or denial of rights — file a complaint with UP Human Rights Commission (Lucknow) or National Human Rights Commission (NHRC, New Delhi) at nhrc.nic.in.

Rule: Always submit complaints in writing and keep copies with date and acknowledgement.

Emergency situations — what to do RIGHT NOW if you or someone is in danger

If you or someone else is in immediate danger — being attacked, kidnapped, threatened with a weapon, or facing any life-threatening situation — follow these steps:

STEP 1 — Call 112 immediately:
UP 112 is available 24x7, every day. GPS tracking is active — your location is identified even if you cannot speak. A Police Response Vehicle (PRV) reaches cities in 10–15 minutes and rural areas in 20–30 minutes. If you cannot talk, keep the line open — operators can hear what is happening. One call to 112 also coordinates ambulance (108) and fire services (101).

STEP 2 — For women: Call 1090:
1090 is UP's dedicated Mahila Helpline. Available 24x7. Handles harassment, stalking, domestic violence, rape, and any emergency involving women. Anonymous complaints are accepted. Immediate police dispatch is activated for life-threatening situations.

STEP 3 — Get to physical safety first:
Your life is more important than filing an FIR. Move to a safe location — a neighbor's house, a shop, any public place. Do not remain in a dangerous location to collect evidence.

STEP 4 — Medical help:
Call 108 for ambulance. Seek medical treatment immediately if injured. At the hospital, ask the doctor for an MLC (Medico-Legal Certificate). This is critical evidence for your FIR.

STEP 5 — Preserve evidence:
Once safe, photograph injuries, crime scene, damaged property. Do not change clothes if there has been a sexual assault — preserve them as evidence. Note names of any witnesses.

STEP 6 — File FIR:
Go to the nearest police station or call 112 to request police come to you. You can file a Zero FIR at any station regardless of where the crime occurred.

STEP 7 — If local police do not respond:
Call CM Helpline 1076 and report both the crime and the police non-response. This is escalated at the state level.

Q: Can I file an FIR in Hindi?
A: Yes, absolutely. FIR can be filed in Hindi or any regional language. English is not required. The officer must write it in a language you understand and read it back to you before you sign.

Q: What if I left out some details in my FIR?
A: You can give an Additional Statement to the police at any time during the investigation. The FIR itself cannot be changed after signing, but supplementary information can be added through formal additional statements.

Q: Do I need to visit a police station or can I file online?
A: In UP, you can file an online complaint at uppolice.gov.in as a starting point. However, for formal FIR registration, a physical visit or police verification is currently required for most offences. E-FIR is being expanded under BNSS 2023.

Q: Police filed my FIR but investigation is stalled — what to do?
A: File a written complaint to the SP with your FIR number citing the delay. File on CM Helpline 1076 — effective in UP. You can also approach the Magistrate who can direct the investigation officer to expedite the case. If chargesheet is not filed within 60/90 days and accused is in custody, apply for Default Bail.

Q: Do I need a lawyer to file an FIR?
A: No. Filing an FIR is a direct citizen right — no lawyer needed. However, for Magistrate applications (BNSS 175(3)), High Court petitions, or bail applications, having a lawyer is strongly recommended. Free legal aid is available from UPSLSA (0522-2209457).

Q: Can police arrest someone just because I filed an FIR?
A: For cognizable offences, police have the power to arrest without a warrant — but they must have reasons to believe the person committed the crime. Filing an FIR does not automatically mean the accused will be arrested. Police investigate and then decide.

Q: What if the accused is a police officer or influential person?
A: Same law applies. File FIR, escalate to SP, and approach the Magistrate if needed. In UP, you can also approach the Police Complaint Authority or file with the DGP office in Lucknow. NHRC handles human rights violations by police.

text_to_review:
Practical tips for filing an FIR — mistakes to avoid and things to do

WHAT YOU MUST DO:

1. Take a witness with you: Go to the police station with at least one witness — a neighbor, relative, or friend. Their presence discourages the police from refusing and serves as a witness to your visit itself.

2. Note your FIR number: This unique number is essential for tracking your case status online, referencing in court, and any future escalation. Write it down and photograph the FIR copy.

3. Get a Medical Certificate immediately: If you have physical injuries, visit a government hospital and request an MLC (Medico-Legal Certificate) from the doctor. Do this before or immediately after filing the FIR — injuries fade. An MLC is strong evidence in court.

4. Preserve digital evidence: Keep all photographs, videos, screenshots, voice recordings, and chat messages related to the crime on your phone. Back them up to cloud storage immediately. Never delete them.

5. Submit everything in writing: Any complaint to SP, DM, or Magistrate should be in writing. Get an acknowledgement with date and official stamp. Verbal complaints cannot be proven later.

6. Keep copies of all documents: FIR copy, SP complaint, medical report, photographs — keep a photocopy or photograph of everything.

WHAT NOT TO DO:

1. Do not disturb the crime scene: If a serious crime occurred — do not touch, move, or clean anything at the crime scene. Forensic evidence is critical. Call police first.

2. Do not post on social media before police investigation is complete: Naming accused or publishing evidence publicly can compromise the case, alert the accused, and give them grounds to get bail. Wait for legal advice.

3. Do not add false details to strengthen your case: Filing an FIR with false information is a criminal offence under BNS Section 215. Stick to facts only.

4. Do not sign before reading: Read the entire FIR before signing. Ensure every detail is accurate. Request corrections before signing — you cannot easily change the FIR afterward.

5. Never pay money to police: FIR registration is completely free. Any demand for money is bribery — reportable on 1064 (UP Anti-Corruption Helpline).

Cognizable vs. Non-Cognizable Offences — the key distinction for FIR

Understanding this distinction determines whether you get an FIR or an NCR, and how urgently police must act.

Cognizable Offence:
Definition: A crime for which police can arrest a person WITHOUT a court warrant and must investigate without Magistrate's permission — BNSS Section 2(1)(g) [formerly CrPC 2(c)].
FIR requirement: Mandatory. Police cannot refuse.
Examples:
- Murder — BNS Section 103 [IPC 302]
- Rape and sexual assault — BNS Sections 64–73 [IPC 376]
- Kidnapping — BNS Section 137 [IPC 363]
- Dacoity/Robbery — BNS Sections 310, 309 [IPC 395, 390]
- Theft above Rs. 5,000 — BNS Section 303 [IPC 379]
- Domestic violence (serious cases)
- POCSO offences (crimes against children)
- Acid attack — BNS Section 124 [IPC 326A]
- Dowry death — BNS Section 80 [IPC 304B]

Non-Cognizable Offence:
Definition: A crime for which police CANNOT arrest without a warrant and cannot investigate without Magistrate's order — BNSS Section 2(1)(l).
NCR registered: Non-Cognizable Report (NCR) is filed at the station.
Examples:
- Minor assault (no serious injury) — BNS Section 115 [IPC 323]
- Verbal abuse and public nuisance — BNS Section 352 [IPC 504]
- Petty theft below Rs. 5,000
- Defamation — BNS Section 356 [IPC 499]
- Minor trespass

What to do for NCR cases:
1. Get the NCR registered at the police station
2. Approach the Judicial Magistrate under BNSS Section 223 [CrPC 200] with a private complaint
3. Magistrate can order police investigation — converting it to a cognizable case if evidence warrants

Note: If a non-cognizable offence escalates (e.g., minor assault leads to serious injury), the officer in charge can convert the NCR to an FIR.

text_to_review:
Chargesheet — what it is, timeline, and what happens after filing

After FIR is registered and police complete their investigation, they file a formal document called a Police Report — commonly called a 'Chargesheet' — with the Magistrate. This is governed by BNSS Section 193 (formerly CrPC Section 173).

What is a Chargesheet:
A chargesheet is the police's conclusion of investigation. It formally presents the case against the accused to the court. Once filed, the court takes over and the trial process begins.

What a Chargesheet Contains:
- Full names of the complainant (victim) and accused
- Nature of the offence and specific BNS/IPC sections
- Summary of evidence collected — physical, forensic, digital
- List of witnesses and their statements
- Whether the accused is in custody or on bail
- Police recommendation — whether to prosecute or not (if police find insufficient evidence, they file a 'Closure Report' instead)

Deadlines for Filing Chargesheet:
60 days — For standard cognizable cases from date of arrest.
90 days — For offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or 10+ years from date of arrest.
No accused in custody — No strict deadline, but courts expect timely filing.

Consequence of Missing the Deadline:
If police miss the 60 or 90-day deadline while the accused is in custody, the accused gets the right to Default Bail (Statutory Bail) under BNSS Section 187(2) [formerly CrPC 167(2)]. This is a right — the Magistrate must grant it. However, the accused must apply for this bail BEFORE the chargesheet is filed. Once chargesheet is filed, this right expires regardless of how late it was filed.

After Chargesheet is Filed:
1. Magistrate takes cognizance of the offence — BNSS Section 210 [formerly CrPC 190]
2. Summons or warrant issued to accused
3. Accused must appear before court
4. Trial begins — examination of witnesses, arguments, judgment
5. Victim should follow up with the assigned Public Prosecutor

For victims in UP: Track chargesheet filing at uppolice.gov.in. If delayed, file complaint with SP or approach the Magistrate directly.

text_to_review:
Types of bail in India — regular bail, anticipatory bail, and default bail explained

Bail means the temporary release of an arrested person on the condition that they appear in court when required. Under BNSS 2023, bail provisions broadly continue from CrPC but with some updates. There are four main types:

1. Regular Bail — BNSS Section 480 [CrPC 437/439]:
When: After a person has been arrested and is in custody.
For bailable offences: Bail is a legal right — police must grant it at the station itself without court intervention.
For non-bailable offences: Bail is discretionary — Magistrate (for lesser offences) or Sessions Court/High Court (for serious offences) decides based on: nature of the crime, criminal history, risk of fleeing, risk of tampering with witnesses or evidence.
How to apply: Through a lawyer at the relevant court. Attach surety details (person who guarantees appearance), ID proof, and address proof.

2. Anticipatory Bail — BNSS Section 482 [CrPC 438]:
When: BEFORE arrest — when a person has reason to believe they may be arrested for a non-bailable offence.
Who grants: Sessions Court or High Court (UP High Court Allahabad).
How to apply: File application through a lawyer. In urgent cases, courts hear it the same day.
Effect: If granted and person is subsequently arrested, they are released on bail at the time of arrest — no time in jail.
Conditions court may impose: Be available for interrogation, not leave India, surrender passport, not influence witnesses.
When to use: False FIR situations, family disputes where police have been approached by the other party, business disputes, political cases.

3. Default Bail (Statutory Bail) — BNSS Section 187(2) [CrPC 167(2)]:
When: Police fail to file chargesheet within 60 days (standard) or 90 days (serious offences) of arrest.
Nature: This is a right, not discretion — Magistrate MUST grant it if conditions are met.
Critical rule: The accused must apply BEFORE chargesheet is filed. Once chargesheet is filed, this right permanently lapses.

4. Interim Bail:
When: Short-term temporary bail while a regular bail application is being heard.
Duration: Usually 7–30 days.
Useful for: Medical emergencies, death of close relative, urgent personal matters during pending bail hearing.

BNSS 2023 — New law replacing CrPC. What changed for FIR and police complaints?

The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023 replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) 1973 from July 1, 2024. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 simultaneously replaced the Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860.

For citizens filing FIRs, the practical process at the police station level remains largely the same. However, these are important new provisions:

1. Electronic FIR (e-FIR) now legally valid — BNSS Section 173(1):
FIRs can now be filed electronically for certain offences. UP is progressively implementing this through uppolice.gov.in. This is especially useful for complainants who cannot physically visit a police station.

2. Mandatory arrest memo — BNSS Section 35:
Police must now prepare a formal arrest memo for every arrest. The memo must be signed by a family member or witness and a copy given to the arrested person. This is a new safeguard against illegal arrests and custodial abuse.

3. Right to inform someone of arrest — BNSS Section 35(3):
Every arrested person has the right to have one person of their choice informed of the arrest and the place of custody. This is now an explicit statutory right — previously it was only a Supreme Court guideline.

4. Trial in absentia for proclaimed offenders — BNSS Section 356:
If an accused continuously evades arrest after being proclaimed an offender, the court can now try and convict them in their absence. This helps victims get justice even when the accused is absconding.

5. Mandatory forensic investigation — BNSS Section 176(3):
For offences punishable with 7 or more years imprisonment, a forensic team must visit the crime scene. This significantly improves evidence quality in serious cases.

6. Section reference mapping (old to new):
CrPC 154 → BNSS 173 (FIR for cognizable offence)
CrPC 156(3) → BNSS 175(3) (Magistrate order for investigation)
CrPC 167 → BNSS 187 (custody and default bail)
CrPC 173 → BNSS 193 (chargesheet/police report)
CrPC 438 → BNSS 482 (anticipatory bail)
CrPC 482 → BNSS 528 (High Court inherent powers)

Note: Both CrPC and BNSS references are widely used in courts and police stations during this transition. Either reference is legally valid.

text_to_review: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 — Overview and Purpose. The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 is a powerful law that protects Dalit (SC) and Adivasi (ST) communities from caste-based violence, discrimination, and social injustice. The Act was passed because older laws like IPC were insufficient to stop caste-based hate crimes. All offenses under this Act are cognizable — police can arrest without warrant. No anticipatory bail is available to the accused. Cases are tried in dedicated Special Courts for faster justice. The Act was strengthened by amendments in 2015 and 2018. Uttar Pradesh has the highest number of SC/ST atrocity cases in India — 23.78% of national cases. National Helpline Against Atrocities: 14566 (24x7, Hindi, English, regional languages).

stated_source: SC/ST Act 1989 Section 2
text_to_review: Who is protected under SC/ST Atrocities Act? Only Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) are protected. SC communities are those listed under Article 341 of Constitution — in UP this includes communities like Chamar, Valmiki, Pasi, Kori, and many others. ST communities are listed under Article 342 — Adivasi communities. Important limitation: The Act only covers offenses by NON-SC/ST persons against SC/ST members. If an SC/ST person commits offense against another SC/ST person, this Act does NOT apply — general IPC applies instead. OBC (Other Backward Classes) are NOT covered under this Act — this is a common misconception. SC/ST certificate from government is required as proof of community identity when filing complaint.

stated_source: SC/ST Act 1989 Section 3
text_to_review: What counts as an atrocity under SC/ST Act? Section 3 defines atrocities in these categories. Physical atrocities: forcing to eat inedible substances, dumping excreta in premises, forcibly removing clothes and parading naked, garlanding with shoes (chappal ki mala), beating, and forcing manual scavenging. Land-related atrocities: wrongfully occupying SC/ST land, dispossessing from land, destroying crops, denying irrigation or forest rights. Social atrocities: imposing social boycott, preventing use of public places or water sources, abusing using caste names (caste slurs) in public view, dedicating SC/ST women as devadasi, preventing from voting. Sexual atrocities: sexual assault on SC/ST woman, sexual exploitation, non-consensual touching. Legal harassment: filing false cases against SC/ST persons. All these are punishable with minimum 6 months to 5 years imprisonment.

stated_source: SC/ST Act 1989 Sections 8, 14, 18, 18A
text_to_review: Special legal features of SC/ST Act — Why it is a powerful law. Cognizable offense: All offenses are cognizable — police can arrest without warrant and investigate without court permission. No anticipatory bail: Accused cannot get pre-arrest bail under Section 18 — this is absolute bar. No preliminary inquiry: After 2018 amendment, police cannot delay FIR by asking for preliminary inquiry — FIR must be registered directly. No senior approval needed: Police officer does not need DSP or SSP approval before making arrest. Presumption of guilt: In certain cases, court presumes accused is guilty — accused must prove innocence. Special Court: Cases must be tried in Exclusive Special Court — UP has 65 such courts. DSP-level investigation: Investigation must be by officer of rank not below Deputy Superintendent of Police.

stated_source: SC/ST Act 1989, CrPC
text_to_review: How to file complaint for SC/ST atrocity? Step 1: Go to nearest police station and file FIR. Since all offenses are cognizable, police MUST register FIR — cannot refuse. File online complaint at uppolice.gov.in. Call National Helpline 14566. File complaint before Magistrate under Section 156(3) CrPC. Contact UP SC/ST Commission at 0522-2236311. Step 3: Investigation must be by DSP-rank officer — if station officer is investigating, you can demand DSP-level officer. Step 4: Case goes to Special Court for trial — not ordinary court. Step 5: Claim victim compensation and relief through District Magistrate office.

stated_source: SC/ST Act 1989 Sections 3, 4
text_to_review: Punishments under SC/ST Atrocities Act. General offenses under Section 3(1): Minimum 6 months, maximum 5 years imprisonment plus fine. Serious IPC offenses committed against SC/ST members (Section 3(2)): Life imprisonment plus fine — applies when underlying IPC offense carries 10+ years. Second and subsequent offenses: Minimum 1 year imprisonment — enhanced penalty for repeat offenders. Public servant neglect of duty: 6 months to 1 year. Property forfeiture: Property used in committing offense may be forfeited. Collective fine: Community that participated in or abetted offense may be collectively fined. These punishments are higher than ordinary IPC — reflecting the serious nature of caste-based violence in Indian context.

The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 and related Indian laws provide comprehensive protection to women against domestic violence, dowry harassment, rape, stalking, and workplace sexual harassment. Any woman facing abuse — whether physical, emotional, sexual, or economic — has strong legal rights and multiple ways to get help. Emotional or verbal abuse — insults, constant humiliation, threats, controlling behavior, preventing from meeting family, public humiliation. Sexual abuse — forcing sexual acts, marital rape, sexual abuse within marriage. Economic abuse — denying money for household needs, preventing woman from working, taking away her salary or property, not allowing access to shared resources.
