text_to_review: Key IPC sections for crimes against women. Note: IPC has been replaced by Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023, but old IPC sections are still widely referenced. IPC 354 / BNS 74: Assault to outrage modesty of woman — 1 to 5 years jail. IPC 354A / BNS 75: Sexual harassment — physical contact, demanding sexual favors — 1 to 3 years. IPC 354B / BNS 76: Assault to disrobe woman — 3 to 7 years. IPC 354C / BNS 77: Voyeurism — 1 to 7 years. IPC 354D / BNS 78: Stalking a woman — 1 to 5 years, repeat offense up to 7 years. IPC 376 / BNS 64: Rape — minimum 7 years, maximum life imprisonment. IPC 498A / BNS 85: Cruelty by husband or relatives — up to 3 years, non-bailable. IPC 509 / BNS 79: Words or gestures to insult modesty of woman — 1 to 3 years. All these are cognizable offenses — police must register FIR.

stated_source: DV Act 2005, IPC, Supreme Court judgments
text_to_review: Frequently asked questions about women safety and domestic violence. Q: Can mother-in-law be included in DV complaint? Yes — DV Act covers all household members including female relatives like mother-in-law, sister-in-law. Q: What if police refuses FIR? Go to SP, file online at uppolice.gov.in, call 1090, or file Section 156(3) application before Magistrate. Q: Can woman file DV case and divorce simultaneously? Yes — both can proceed simultaneously. DV case gives immediate protection and maintenance while divorce proceeds. Q: Is 498A automatically an arrest? Police can arrest without warrant but Supreme Court guidelines ask for some preliminary verification. Filing is still very effective. Q: Can live-in partner file DV complaint? Yes — live-in partners are fully protected under DV Act 2005. Q: What if abuser has political connections? Contact NCW at 7827170170, file online complaint. NCW can directly intervene.

stated_source: DV Act 2005, UP Government
text_to_review: Practical tips for women seeking legal help. Document everything: Photograph injuries immediately before they fade. Save all threatening messages, voice notes, emails. Ask witnesses to give written statements. Keep medical reports carefully. Use 1090 first: UP Mahila Power Line 1090 is the most effective first step in UP — they handle everything from counseling to police action to shelter. Do not delay: Evidence fades over time. Medical examination should happen within 24-48 hours of assault. You have the right to stay in your house: Under DV Act, no one can throw you out of shared household. Get protection order if threatened with eviction. Free help is available: One Stop Centre, UPSLSA, Protection Officer — all free services in UP. You do not need a lawyer to file DV case — Protection Officer can help file application for free. 1090 App available on Google Play Store for quick access.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019
text_to_review: Consumer law in India protects every buyer of goods and services from unfair trade practices, defective products, deficient services, and exploitation by sellers and manufacturers. The main law is the Consumer Protection Act 2019 which replaced the old 1986 Act. Every person who buys goods or hires services for personal use is a consumer with legal rights. This includes purchases from shops, online platforms, hospitals, banks, insurance companies, builders, telecom companies, and government utilities. In Uttar Pradesh, consumer disputes are resolved through a three-tier system: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (DCDRC) at district level, UP State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in Lucknow, and National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) in New Delhi. Filing a consumer complaint is simple, inexpensive, and does not require a lawyer. The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) set up under the 2019 Act can take suo motu action against companies for widespread unfair practices. UP has District Consumer Forums in all 75 districts.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Section 2(7)
text_to_review: Who is a consumer under the Consumer Protection Act 2019? A consumer is any person who buys goods or hires services for personal use and not for resale or commercial purpose. Online buyers are also consumers. A person who buys goods as a gift is also a consumer. If you buy goods for running a business you are NOT a consumer under this Act. Beneficiaries of services are covered even if they did not directly pay — for example a patient treated under someone else's insurance. NRIs who buy goods or services in India are covered. Who is NOT a consumer: a person who buys goods for resale; a person in an employer-employee relationship getting services; persons availing completely free services. The 2019 Act widened the definition to include all electronic and online transactions. In UP, any resident who has purchased goods or availed services and faced deficiency can approach the District Consumer Forum of their district without needing to hire a lawyer.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Section 2
text_to_review: What are the six fundamental rights of every consumer in India? Right 1 — Right to Safety: protection against goods and services hazardous to life and property. Right 2 — Right to Information: the right to know the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard, and price of goods and services before buying. Right 3 — Right to Choose: access to variety of goods and services at competitive prices. Right 4 — Right to be Heard: assurance that consumer interests receive proper attention at appropriate forums. Right 5 — Right to Seek Redressal: right to seek settlement of genuine grievances against unfair trade practices or exploitation. Right 6 — Right to Consumer Education: the right to acquire knowledge and skills to be an informed consumer. These six rights are enshrined in the Consumer Protection Act 2019 and form the foundation of all consumer protection in India. In UP, the Consumer Awareness programmes under Jaago Grahak Jaago campaign are run by the Department of Consumer Affairs to educate citizens about these rights.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Section 2(6), 2(11), 2(47)
text_to_review: What kind of complaints can be filed under Consumer Protection Act 2019? Defective goods: goods that are faulty, substandard, or do not conform to promised quality. Deficient services: services falling short of the standard promised — poor hospital treatment, bad contractor work, bank errors. Unfair trade practices: misleading advertisements, false claims, selling above MRP, refusing to issue bills, bait and switch tactics. Overcharging: charging more than MRP or agreed price. Selling hazardous goods without proper warnings. Unfair contracts: one-sided contract clauses that disadvantage consumers. Online fraud and e-commerce cheating: fake products, non-delivery, refund denial. Medical negligence, builder delays, insurance claim rejection, and telecom service failure are also covered. In UP, common complaints include: shops charging above MRP; private hospitals overcharging; builders delaying flat possession in Noida, Greater Noida, Lucknow; insurance companies rejecting claims; banks making unauthorized deductions. All these can be filed at the District Consumer Forum of the relevant district in UP.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Section 34, 47, 58
text_to_review: Which consumer forum should you approach and what are the monetary limits in UP? District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (District Forum): handles complaints where value of goods or services and compensation claimed is up to Rs 50 lakh. In UP, all 75 districts have a District Consumer Forum. State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (State Commission): handles complaints where value exceeds Rs 50 lakh but is up to Rs 2 crore. UP State Consumer Commission is located in Lucknow — address: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission UP, Vibhuti Khand, Gomti Nagar, Lucknow. National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC): handles complaints where value exceeds Rs 2 crore, located in New Delhi. Appeals: District Forum order can be appealed to State Commission within 45 days; State Commission to NCDRC within 30 days; NCDRC to Supreme Court within 30 days. Filing fees are nominal and increase with claim value. For UP consumers, the District Forum in their own district is the most accessible starting point.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019 Section 35, e-Daakhil Portal edaakhil.nic.in
text_to_review: How to file a consumer complaint in Uttar Pradesh? Step 1: Send a legal notice to the seller or service provider by registered post demanding remedy within 15 to 30 days. Keep a copy. Step 2: If no satisfactory response, file complaint at the District Consumer Forum of your district or online at edaakhil.nic.in. Step 3: The complaint must include your name and address, name and address of opposite party, facts of the case in chronological order, supporting documents such as bill, warranty card, photographs, and correspondence, and relief claimed such as replacement, refund, or compensation. Step 4: Pay filing fee — up to Rs 5 lakh claim fee is Rs 200; Rs 5 lakh to Rs 10 lakh fee is Rs 400; Rs 10 lakh to Rs 20 lakh fee is Rs 500; Rs 20 lakh to Rs 50 lakh fee is Rs 2,000. Step 5: File in person at the District Consumer Forum office or online at edaakhil.nic.in. A lawyer is not required. In UP, the e-Daakhil portal has made filing complaints from home possible for all UP residents without visiting the forum office.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Section 35(1), 58, 69, Consumer Protection (Mediation) Regulations 2020
text_to_review: What are the time limits for consumer complaints in UP? The consumer complaint must be filed within 2 years from the date the cause of action arose — meaning from the date of defect, deficiency, or unfair practice. If filed after 2 years, the consumer must explain the delay and the forum may condone it if satisfied with the reason. Once a complaint is filed, the District Forum must decide it within 3 months if no lab testing is required and within 5 months if lab testing is needed. The 2019 Act introduced strict timelines to prevent delays which were rampant under the old 1986 Act. Appeal against District Forum order must be filed within 45 days. Appeal against State Commission order must be filed within 30 days. The new 2019 Act also introduced mediation — the forum may refer cases to mediation at Consumer Mediation Cells attached to each Commission for faster resolution. UP State Commission in Lucknow has an active mediation cell. Mediation settlements are passed as orders of the Consumer Commission and are final and binding.

stated_source: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020, Consumer Protection Act 2019
text_to_review: What are consumer rights in online shopping and e-commerce in India? The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 specifically protect online shoppers. Every e-commerce platform like Amazon, Flipkart, Meesho, Myntra must: display country of origin of all goods; display seller name and contact information clearly; not manipulate prices unfairly; have a clear return and refund policy displayed prominently; not cancel orders without consumer consent; acknowledge complaints within 48 hours and resolve within 1 month. Fake reviews, misleading product descriptions, and hidden charges are prohibited. If an online seller delivers a defective or wrong product, the consumer can demand full refund or replacement. If the platform refuses, file a complaint against both the seller and the platform at the District Consumer Forum or at consumerhelpline.gov.in. The National Consumer Helpline 1800-11-4000 has tie-ups with major e-commerce companies for faster resolution. UP consumers buying from online platforms can file their complaint at the District Consumer Forum of their own district.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Indian Medical Council Regulations, UP Health Department
text_to_review: What are consumer rights in case of medical negligence in UP? Medical services are covered under the Consumer Protection Act 2019. Patients and families are consumers; hospitals, doctors, nursing homes, and diagnostic labs are service providers. If a doctor or hospital is negligent resulting in wrong treatment, wrong diagnosis, surgical errors, or death, a consumer complaint can be filed at the District Consumer Forum. The complaint can seek compensation for cost of treatment, loss of income, mental agony, and in case of death, compensation to dependants. Expert medical opinion is often required to prove negligence. Important UP-specific points: complaints against government hospitals can also be filed with the UP Health Department or Chief Medical Officer of the district; private hospital overcharging complaints can be filed with the UP Private Hospital Regulatory Authority; any hospital denying emergency treatment to accident or assault victims can be reported to the CMO. Free services at government hospitals are not covered under Consumer Protection Act — patients using paid services at government hospitals are covered. Consumer complaints against Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra government medical colleges can be filed at the respective District Consumer Forum.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Insurance Ombudsman Rules 2017, IRDAI Bima Bharosa
text_to_review: What are consumer rights regarding insurance claim rejection in UP? Insurance services are fully covered under the Consumer Protection Act 2019. If an insurance company wrongfully rejects a claim, delays settlement, pays less than entitled, or misrepresents policy terms, the policyholder can take action. Escalation steps: first raise complaint with the insurance company grievance redressal cell; if unresolved within 30 days, approach the Insurance Ombudsman. For UP residents, the Insurance Ombudsman for Lucknow region covers all UP districts — office at Jeevan Bhawan Phase II, 6th Floor, Nawal Kishore Road, Hazratganj, Lucknow; email bimaou.lucknow@gmail.com; phone 0522-2231331. If still unresolved or claim exceeds Ombudsman limits, file at District Consumer Forum. IRDAI Bima Bharosa portal at bimabharosa.irdai.gov.in also accepts complaints. IRDAI Bima Bharosa helpline: 155255. Motor accident insurance disputes can go to both MACT and Consumer Forum. Health insurance claim rejections are among the most common consumer complaints in UP — always read policy exclusions carefully and keep all hospital bills and discharge summaries.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, RERA Act 2016, UP-RERA, up-rera.in
text_to_review: What can homebuyers do if a builder delays possession or cheats in UP? Builder and real estate complaints in UP are covered under two laws: Consumer Protection Act 2019 and RERA (Real Estate Regulatory Authority) Act 2016. Under UP-RERA: if a builder delays possession beyond the agreed date, the buyer is entitled to interest at SBI MCLR plus 2% for every month of delay; if builder fails to deliver, buyer can claim full refund with interest. File RERA complaint at UP-RERA Lucknow — website up-rera.in; helpline 0522-2238494; office at RERA Bhawan, Vibhuti Khand, Gomti Nagar, Lucknow. Under Consumer Protection Act: file at District Consumer Forum for deficient service including poor construction quality, false advertisements about amenities, and delayed possession. Both RERA and Consumer Forum complaints can be filed simultaneously. UP has one of the highest volumes of builder complaints in India especially in Noida, Greater Noida, Lucknow, Ghaziabad, and Agra. The Allahabad High Court has passed several judgments directing UP-RERA to expedite builder complaint resolution.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021
text_to_review: What are consumer rights against banks and NBFCs in UP? Banking and financial services are fully covered under Consumer Protection Act 2019. Common complaints include: unauthorized debit or transaction, ATM cash not dispensed but account debited, loan disbursement issues, excessive charges, wrongful cheque bounce, credit card fraud, account freezing without notice, and poor locker service. Escalation steps: first file complaint with the bank branch manager; then escalate to the bank's nodal officer; if unresolved within 30 days, approach the RBI Integrated Ombudsman at bankingombudsman.rbi.org.in or call 14448 toll free — covers all commercial banks, cooperative banks, and NBFCs. For UP, the RBI Regional Office in Lucknow also handles escalated complaints. For compensation claims, file consumer complaint at District Consumer Forum. Digital payment fraud must be reported immediately to the bank and at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930. RBI has mandated that banks must resolve complaints within 30 days — if they fail, they must pay compensation of Rs 100 per day of delay beyond 30 days. Keep all transaction references and correspondence as evidence.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, TRAI Telecom Consumer Protection Regulations 2012
text_to_review: What are consumer rights against telecom companies in UP? Telecom companies like Jio, Airtel, BSNL, and Vi are service providers under Consumer Protection Act 2019. Common complaints: excess billing, unauthorized balance deductions, poor network or internet quality, wrongful SIM disconnection, number portability refusal, and SIM swap fraud. Escalation steps: Step 1 — raise complaint with company customer care and get a complaint reference number; Step 2 — if unresolved within 30 days, escalate to the telecom company's Appellate Authority; Step 3 — if still unresolved, file complaint with TRAI at pgportal.gov.in or call TRAI helpline 1800-110-420; Step 4 — for compensation, file consumer complaint at District Consumer Forum. BSNL complaints in UP can also be raised at the BSNL UP Circle office in Lucknow. For mobile number misuse or fraudulent calls, report at Sanchar Saathi portal sancharsaathi.gov.in. For disconnection of mobile number wrongfully, TRAI regulations require restoration within 24 hours of resolution. UP has large BSNL rural coverage — BSNL service complaints from rural UP are common and should be escalated to TRAI if unresolved.

stated_source: Food Safety and Standards Act 2006, FSSAI, UP Food Safety and Drug Administration
text_to_review: What are consumer rights regarding food adulteration and substandard food in UP? The Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 (FSSAI Act) governs food safety across India. Selling adulterated, misbranded, or substandard food is a serious offence with penalties up to life imprisonment for adulteration causing death. How to report in UP: file complaint with the Food Safety Officer (FSO) of your district under the UP Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA); file complaint on FSSAI portal at foscos.fssai.gov.in; file consumer complaint at District Consumer Forum for compensation. UP FSDA office is in Lucknow — helpline 1800-180-5533. Common adulteration issues in UP: milk adulteration with urea or detergent; synthetic sweets especially during festival seasons; adulterated mustard oil and ghee; substandard spices and pulses. The UP government conducts regular food sampling drives especially before Holi, Diwali, and Eid. Consumers can demand the FBO (Food Business Operator) license of any food establishment before buying. Restaurants and dhabas must display FSSAI license number. Buying food from unlicensed vendors carries risk — complaints about such vendors go to the local FSO.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Chapter VI, Section 82-87
text_to_review: What is product liability under the Consumer Protection Act 2019? The Consumer Protection Act 2019 for the first time expressly recognizes product liability in India. A manufacturer, seller, or service provider can be held liable for harm caused by a defective product or deficient service without the consumer needing to prove negligence. Grounds for product liability claim: manufacturing defect; failure to conform to express warranty; inadequate instructions for use; unreasonably dangerous product design. Compensation can be claimed for personal injury, property damage, and death caused by the defective product. This applies to all products sold in India including imported goods. Common UP product liability cases include: spurious medicines sold at pharmacies; defective electrical appliances causing fire or injury; contaminated packaged food; defective LPG cylinders causing accidents. For spurious medicines, complaint also goes to UP Drug Controller at UP FSDA. For defective LPG cylinders, complaint goes to the oil company distributor and simultaneously to the District Consumer Forum. Product liability claims are filed at the District Consumer Forum for claims up to Rs 50 lakh.

stated_source: Legal Metrology Act 2009, Consumer Protection Act 2019, CCPA Guidelines
text_to_review: What are the rules on MRP, weights, and measures and how to complain in UP? MRP (Maximum Retail Price) is the highest price at which a product can be sold to the end consumer — no shopkeeper or seller can charge above MRP. This is governed by the Legal Metrology Act 2009 and the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules 2011. Rules every consumer should know: every packaged commodity must display MRP, net quantity, date of manufacture, expiry date, and manufacturer details; selling above MRP is a criminal offence; weighing scales must be government-stamped and calibrated; selling less than stated quantity is an offence. How to complain in UP: file complaint with the Legal Metrology Officer of the district (under UP Weights and Measures Department); file consumer complaint at District Consumer Forum; for MRP violations at large retail chains, also report to the Central Consumer Protection Authority at consumerhelpline.gov.in. Common UP violations: hotels and restaurants charging above MRP on bottled water and beverages — this is illegal; cinemas charging above MRP on water and food is also illegal as clarified by NCDRC. Hotels in Lucknow, Agra, Varanasi are frequently penalized for MRP violations.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Section 2(47), CCPA Guidelines on Misleading Advertisements 2022
text_to_review: What are unfair trade practices and how are consumers protected? Under Consumer Protection Act 2019, unfair trade practices include: false representation that goods are of a particular standard, quality, or grade when they are not; false claim about sponsorship, approval, or affiliation; false representation about price savings or discounts; conducting prize schemes or contests with intent not to give the promised prize; withholding information about defects in goods; issuing false warranties or guarantees. Misleading advertisements are specifically addressed — the CCPA (Central Consumer Protection Authority) can: order withdrawal of misleading advertisements; ban the advertiser from advertising for up to 1 year; impose penalty up to Rs 10 lakh on manufacturer and up to Rs 10 lakh on celebrity endorser. Common unfair practices in UP: fake gold schemes and chit funds promising unrealistic returns; real estate advertisements showing amenities never delivered; tour operators selling packages with hidden charges; coaching institutes in Prayagraj and Lucknow making false placement claims. Complaints about unfair trade practices can be filed at consumerhelpline.gov.in, CCPA, or the District Consumer Forum.

stated_source: National Consumer Helpline, Department of Consumer Affairs, Government of India
text_to_review: What is the National Consumer Helpline and how to use it? The National Consumer Helpline (NCH) is run by the Government of India to help consumers resolve complaints before approaching Consumer Forums. Helpline: 1800-11-4000 or 14404 — toll free, Monday to Saturday 8 AM to 8 PM. Online portal: consumerhelpline.gov.in — file complaints for all types of consumer grievances. The portal has tie-ups with over 1000 companies including major e-commerce, telecom, banking, insurance, and FMCG companies for faster resolution. In UP, the State Consumer Helpline also operates. The Jaago Grahak Jaago mobile app also allows complaint filing. If the company resolves the complaint through the helpline, there is no need to go to the Consumer Forum. For complaints not resolved through NCH, the consumer can escalate to the District Consumer Forum. UP District Consumer Forum addresses and contact details are available at consumerhelpline.gov.in. CCPA also accepts complaints about systemic unfair practices affecting large numbers of consumers. All services are free of cost for consumers.

stated_source: e-Daakhil Portal edaakhil.nic.in, Consumer Protection Act 2019
text_to_review: What is the e-Daakhil portal and how does it work for UP consumers? e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in) is the official online portal for filing consumer complaints in India, launched by the Government of India in 2020. It allows consumers to file complaints, pay fees, upload documents, track case status, and attend hearings online without physically visiting the Consumer Forum. How to file on e-Daakhil: register at edaakhil.nic.in with mobile number and email; select the state (Uttar Pradesh) and the District Consumer Forum of your district; fill complaint details including opposite party information, facts, and relief sought; upload supporting documents such as bills, warranty cards, and correspondence; pay filing fee online via UPI, debit card, or net banking; on submission, a unique complaint number is issued for tracking. Hearings can be attended via video conferencing. Case status can be tracked online using the complaint number. This portal is especially useful for UP consumers in smaller districts like Sonbhadra, Chitrakoot, Shravasti, and Balrampur who would otherwise have to travel long distances to file complaints. e-Daakhil is available 24x7. All 75 District Consumer Forums in UP are connected to the e-Daakhil system.

stated_source: Consumer Protection Act 2019, UP-RERA, UP FSDA, Insurance Ombudsman Lucknow, RBI Ombudsman
text_to_review: Common real life consumer law situations in UP and where to go. Bought defective mobile from Lucknow or Kanpur shop — send legal notice, then file at District Consumer Forum for replacement or refund. Online order not delivered and refund denied — file at consumerhelpline.gov.in or District Consumer Forum against both seller and platform. Private hospital overcharged or negligent treatment in UP — file at District Consumer Forum for refund and compensation. Insurance claim wrongfully rejected — approach Insurance Ombudsman Lucknow first at 0522-2231331, then District Consumer Forum. Builder delayed flat possession in Noida, Greater Noida, or Lucknow — file with UP-RERA at up-rera.in and simultaneously at District Consumer Forum. Bank debited money wrongfully — report to bank, if unresolved file at RBI Ombudsman bankingombudsman.rbi.org.in or call 14448. Expired food product sold at supermarket — report to UP FSDA on 1800-180-5533 and file consumer complaint. Telecom company deducting balance illegally — escalate to TRAI at pgportal.gov.in. Shop charging above MRP — report to Legal Metrology Officer and file at District Consumer Forum. All consumer complaints can also be filed online at edaakhil.nic.in from home.

stated_source: Minimum Wages Act 1948, Industrial Disputes Act 1947, Labour Codes 2019-2020
text_to_review: Labour law in India protects the rights of workers in both organized and unorganized sectors. Every worker whether in a factory, shop, construction site, domestic work, or agriculture has legal rights related to wages, working hours, safety, and termination. In Uttar Pradesh, both Central Government laws (applicable nationwide) and UP State Government laws apply together. Key central laws include the Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Wages Act 1936, Factories Act 1948, Industrial Disputes Act 1947, and the new Labour Codes (2019-2020). Key UP-specific laws include the UP Shops and Commercial Establishments Act 1962 and UP Industrial Disputes Act provisions. Workers can file complaints with Labour Department UP, Labour Court, or approach the Assistant Labour Commissioner of their district.

stated_source: Minimum Wages Act 1948, UP Labour Department Notification 2024
text_to_review: What is minimum wage and what are the current rates in UP? Every employer must pay at least the minimum wage fixed by the government, paying less is a criminal offence. Minimum wages in Uttar Pradesh are revised periodically by the UP Labour Department. As of 2024, UP minimum wages are: Unskilled workers approximately Rs 10,285 per month; Semi-skilled approximately Rs 11,385 per month; Skilled approximately Rs 12,545 per month; Highly skilled approximately Rs 13,505 per month. These rates vary by industry and are revised twice yearly in April and October. Minimum wages apply to all workers including domestic workers, construction workers, agricultural workers, shop employees, and factory workers. If an employer pays less than minimum wage, the worker can file a complaint with the Assistant Labour Commissioner of the district. The employer can be fined up to Rs 500 and sentenced to 6 months imprisonment.

stated_source: Payment of Wages Act 1936, Section 3, 7, 15
text_to_review: What are the rules for payment of wages? Under the Payment of Wages Act 1936, wages must be paid on time. For establishments with fewer than 1000 workers, wages must be paid by the 7th of every month; for larger establishments, by the 10th. Wages cannot be deducted except for: absence from duty, damage caused, advance taken, income tax, PF contribution, and ESI contribution. Deductions cannot exceed 50% of wages in a month (75% in case of debt repayment). Wages must be paid in cash or by bank transfer, payment in kind is not allowed. Any unauthorized deduction or delay in wages can be reported to the Inspector under Payment of Wages Act. The employer can be penalized with fine up to Rs 7,500. For UP workers, complaints go to the Assistant Labour Commissioner of the concerned district.

stated_source: Factories Act 1948 Section 51-56, UP Shops and Commercial Establishments Act 1962
text_to_review: What are the legal working hours for workers? Under the Factories Act 1948, a worker in a factory cannot be made to work more than 9 hours per day and 48 hours per week. Overtime is allowed but must be paid at double the ordinary wage rate. Weekly rest of at least one day is mandatory. Spread-over of work cannot exceed 10.5 hours in a day. Women workers cannot be employed between 7 PM and 6 AM in factories. For shops and commercial establishments in UP, the UP Shops and Commercial Establishments Act 1962 applies: maximum 9 hours per day and 54 hours per week; one day off per week mandatory. Any employee working on a weekly holiday must be given a substitute holiday or double wages. Violation of working hour rules can be reported to the Factory Inspector or Assistant Labour Commissioner.

stated_source: EPF Act 1952, ESI Act 1948
text_to_review: What are PF and ESI and who is entitled to them? Provident Fund (PF): Under the Employees Provident Fund Act 1952, every establishment with 20 or more employees must enroll workers in EPFO. Employee contributes 12% of basic salary; employer also contributes 12%. Workers can check PF balance on the EPFO portal epfindia.gov.in or by missed call to 011-22901406. PF can be withdrawn on retirement, resignation after 2 months of unemployment, medical emergency, home purchase, or child education. ESI (Employee State Insurance): Under the ESI Act 1948, workers earning up to Rs 21,000 per month in establishments with 10 or more employees are entitled to ESI. Employee contributes 0.75% of wages; employer contributes 3.25%. ESI provides free medical treatment, sickness benefit of 70% wages during illness, maternity benefit for 26 weeks, disability benefit, and dependent benefit. Complaints of PF or ESI denial can be filed with Regional PF Commissioner UP or ESIC Regional Office Lucknow.

stated_source: Industrial Disputes Act 1947, Section 25F, 25N, Chapter VB
text_to_review: What are the rules for termination and retrenchment of workers? For workers with 1 year or more of continuous service in establishments with 100 or more workers, the employer must obtain prior permission from the government before retrenchment or closure, this is called Chapter VB of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947. For establishments with fewer than 100 workers, one month notice or payment in lieu of notice must be given. Retrenchment compensation is 15 days average pay for every completed year of service. Workers cannot be dismissed for trade union activity or going on legal strike. In UP, wrongful termination can be challenged before the Labour Court by filing an industrial dispute. The complaint must be filed within 3 years of termination. Additionally, any worker dismissed without proper procedure can demand reinstatement with back wages through the Labour Court.

stated_source: Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, Section 4, 7
text_to_review: What is gratuity and who is eligible? Gratuity is a lump sum amount paid by an employer to an employee as recognition for services rendered. Under the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, every employee who has completed 5 or more years of continuous service is entitled to gratuity on resignation, retirement, death, or disablement. The formula is: Gratuity equals last drawn basic salary plus DA multiplied by 15 divided by 26 multiplied by number of years of service. The maximum gratuity payable is Rs 20 lakh as amended in 2018. For death or disability, the 5-year rule is waived. Gratuity must be paid within 30 days of it becoming due, delay attracts simple interest at 10% per annum. If employer refuses to pay gratuity, the worker can file a complaint with the Controlling Authority which is the Assistant Labour Commissioner in UP. Gratuity is tax-exempt up to Rs 20 lakh for both government and private sector employees.

stated_source: Maternity Benefit Act 1961, Amendment 2017
text_to_review: What maternity benefits are women workers entitled to? Under the Maternity Benefit Act 1961 amended in 2017, every woman employee who has worked for at least 80 days in the last 12 months is entitled to: 26 weeks of paid maternity leave for the first two children; 12 weeks for the third child onwards; 12 weeks for mothers adopting a child below 3 months; 6 weeks in case of miscarriage or medical termination. The employer must pay the woman her full average daily wage during maternity leave. Creche facility is mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees. A nursing break of 2 intervals per day is allowed. A woman cannot be dismissed or discharged during maternity leave. Complaints of denial of maternity benefits can be filed with the Inspector under the Act or the Assistant Labour Commissioner in UP. Employers who violate maternity benefit rules can be imprisoned for up to 1 year and fined up to Rs 5,000.

stated_source: Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act 2016
text_to_review: What is the law on child labour in India and UP? Under the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act 2016, employment of children below 14 years is completely prohibited in all occupations and industries. Children between 14 and 18 years known as adolescents are prohibited from working in hazardous occupations like mines, factories, and construction. Adolescents can work in non-hazardous work but not during school hours and not more than 3 hours per day. Children can help in family-run businesses or in entertainment after school hours. The penalty for employing a child below 14 years is imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years and fine of Rs 20,000 to Rs 50,000. Repeat offences attract higher penalties. In UP, complaints of child labour can be filed with the District Labour Office, Childline at 1098, or UP Police. The District Magistrate has special powers to rescue child labourers.

stated_source: Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976, Central Sector Scheme for Rehabilitation
text_to_review: What is bonded labour and what protections exist? Bonded labour also called bandhua mazdoori is a form of forced labour where a worker is bound to work for an employer to repay a debt, often under threat or coercion. Bonded labour is completely abolished in India under the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976. Any bonded labour agreement is void and unenforceable. The bonded worker cannot be forced to repay the debt. District Magistrates are responsible for identifying, releasing, and rehabilitating bonded labourers. Released bonded labourers are entitled to rehabilitation assistance under the Central Sector Scheme: up to Rs 1 lakh for individuals and Rs 2 lakh for families. In UP, complaints of bonded labour can be filed with the District Magistrate, District Labour Office, or UP Police. The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) also takes cognizance of bonded labour cases.

stated_source: BOCW Act 1996, UP Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board
text_to_review: What special rights do construction workers have in UP? Construction workers are covered under the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act 1996. Every construction worker who has worked for at least 90 days in the past 12 months must be registered with the UP Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board at upbocw.in. Benefits for registered construction workers in UP include: financial assistance of Rs 15,000 for marriage of daughters; scholarship for children's education; maternity benefit of Rs 12,000; medical assistance up to Rs 5 lakh; accident compensation up to Rs 1 lakh; pension after retirement; financial assistance for tools and equipment. The construction employer must pay 1% of total construction cost as cess to the welfare fund. Registration is done online at upbocw.in. An unregistered construction worker loses access to all these benefits.

stated_source: Unorganised Workers Social Security Act 2008, Minimum Wages Act 1948
text_to_review: What are the rights of domestic workers in UP? Domestic workers including maids, cooks, drivers, and gardeners employed in households are among the most vulnerable workers. There is no dedicated Central law for domestic workers yet, but they are protected under several provisions. UP is yet to notify a specific state policy for domestic workers. However, domestic workers are entitled to minimum wages under the Minimum Wages Act 1948 if notified in the state schedule. They are protected from bonded labour, forced labour, and physical abuse under IPC. They can report workplace abuse or withheld wages to the local police or District Labour Office. The Unorganised Workers Social Security Act 2008 provides for registration of domestic workers as unorganised workers so they can access welfare schemes like Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maandhan (PM-SYM), a pension scheme for unorganised workers earning less than Rs 15,000 per month. Workers can enroll via Jan Seva Kendra.

stated_source: POSH Act 2013, IPC Section 354
text_to_review: What is the law on sexual harassment at the workplace? The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act 2013, commonly called the POSH Act, protects every woman worker from sexual harassment at any workplace including offices, factories, shops, hospitals, educational institutions, and even domestic work. Every employer with 10 or more employees must constitute an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC). The complaint must be filed within 3 months of the incident. The ICC must complete inquiry within 90 days. If the complaint is found valid, the employer must take action ranging from written apology to termination and compensation. For workplaces with fewer than 10 workers or against the employer himself, complaints go to the Local Complaints Committee (LCC) formed by the District Officer. In UP, the District Officer at district headquarters oversees LCCs. Victims can also file a criminal complaint under IPC Section 354 for outraging modesty.

stated_source: Code on Wages 2019, Industrial Relations Code 2020, Social Security Code 2020, OSH Code 2020
text_to_review: What are the new Labour Codes and how do they affect workers? The Government of India consolidated 29 central labour laws into 4 Labour Codes between 2019 and 2020: First, the Code on Wages 2019 covers minimum wages, payment of wages, bonus, and equal remuneration for all workers including unorganised sector. Second, the Industrial Relations Code 2020 covers trade unions, industrial disputes, and standing orders. Third, the Social Security Code 2020 covers PF, ESI, gratuity, maternity benefit, and social security for gig and platform workers. Fourth, the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020 covers safety, working hours, and conditions across all industries. As of 2024, the Labour Codes have been passed by Parliament but not yet fully implemented as states including UP are still drafting their rules. Until implementation, the old laws continue to apply. Workers should follow existing laws while staying aware that codes may bring changes.

stated_source: Industrial Disputes Act 1947, UP Labour Department
text_to_review: How to file a labour complaint in Uttar Pradesh? Step 1: Identify the right authority. For wage disputes and minimum wages go to the Assistant Labour Commissioner of your district. For PF complaints go to the Regional PF Commissioner at the EPFO office. For ESI complaints go to ESIC Regional Office Lucknow. For factory safety violations go to the Factory Inspector of the district. For child labour complaints go to the District Labour Officer or call Childline at 1098. For wrongful termination go to the Labour Court of the district. Step 2: File a written complaint with details of the employer, nature of violation, and proof if available. Step 3: The Labour Department must conduct an inquiry. Step 4: If unsatisfied with Labour Department action, approach the Labour Court by filing an industrial dispute. You do not need a lawyer for this, a union representative or the worker himself can file. UP Labour Department helpline: 1800-180-5412 toll free. Online complaint portal: upsamadhan.in or jansunwai.up.nic.in.

stated_source: UP Shops and Commercial Establishments Act 1962
text_to_review: What is the UP Shops and Commercial Establishments Act 1962 and who does it cover? The UP Shops and Commercial Establishments Act 1962 governs all shops, hotels, restaurants, eating houses, theatres, cinemas, and other commercial establishments in Uttar Pradesh. It does not apply to factories covered by the Factories Act or government offices. Key provisions include: maximum 9 hours of work per day and 54 hours per week; one day of weekly rest is mandatory; overtime must be paid at double rate; workers are entitled to annual leave at 1 day for every 20 days of work; the establishment must be registered with the local municipality or UP Labour Department; workers cannot be dismissed without one month notice or salary in lieu of notice; women and young workers cannot be employed after 10 PM. Violations can be reported to the Chief Inspector of Shops and Establishments in the district.

stated_source: Trade Unions Act 1926, Industrial Disputes Act 1947 Section 25T
text_to_review: What are the rights of trade unions and workers to organize? Under the Trade Unions Act 1926, any 7 or more workers can form a trade union and get it registered with the Registrar of Trade Unions. A registered trade union has the right to negotiate with the employer collectively through collective bargaining. Registered trade unions are protected from civil and criminal prosecution for legitimate trade union activities. Workers cannot be dismissed or victimized for being a member of or forming a trade union, which is an Unfair Labour Practice under the Industrial Disputes Act. Workers have the right to go on strike but for establishments classified as public utility services, 14 days advance notice must be given. In UP, the Registrar of Trade Unions office is in Lucknow. Common UP trade union registrations cover textile, brick kiln, construction, transport, and agricultural workers.

stated_source: Unorganised Workers Social Security Act 2008, e-Shram portal, PM-SYM
text_to_review: What benefits are available to unorganised workers in UP? Unorganised workers including street vendors, rickshaw pullers, daily wage labourers, agricultural workers, and home-based workers are covered under the Unorganised Workers Social Security Act 2008. Key government schemes available to them: PM Shram Yogi Maandhan (PM-SYM) provides pension of Rs 3,000 per month after 60 years for workers earning less than Rs 15,000 per month; Ayushman Bharat provides free health insurance up to Rs 5 lakh per year for eligible families; PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana provides life insurance of Rs 2 lakh at Rs 436 per year; PM Suraksha Bima Yojana provides accident insurance of Rs 2 lakh at Rs 20 per year; e-Shram card is a national database of unorganised workers that also provides Rs 2 lakh accident insurance free. Register at eshram.gov.in or any Jan Seva Kendra. UP Labour Department runs special camps for registration.

stated_source: Equal Remuneration Act 1976, Code on Wages 2019
text_to_review: Is there a law against wage discrimination on the basis of gender? Yes. The Equal Remuneration Act 1976, now subsumed under the Code on Wages 2019, mandates equal pay for equal work regardless of gender. An employer cannot pay a woman worker less than a male worker for the same or similar work. Discrimination in recruitment on the basis of gender is also prohibited except in jobs where the government specifically permits it. Violations can be reported to the Labour Department. The employer can be fined between Rs 10,000 and Rs 20,000 for first offence and imprisoned for 2 years for repeat offences. In practice, wage discrimination against women remains common especially in agriculture and unorganised sectors in UP. Women workers are advised to document wage discrepancies and file complaints with the Assistant Labour Commissioner of the district.

text_to_review: Common real life labour law situations in UP and where to go. Employer not paying minimum wage: complain to Assistant Labour Commissioner of district. Salary delayed beyond 7th or 10th of month: complaint under Payment of Wages Act to Labour Inspector. text_to_review:
Property and Land Disputes in Uttar Pradesh — Overview

Property disputes in UP fall under several laws depending on the type of dispute. Understanding which law applies is the first step.

For agricultural land and village land: The UP Revenue Code 2006 and the UP Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act 1950 govern all land records, mutation, encroachment, and tenure rights. The basic land documents are: Khatauni (Record of Rights — who owns which plot), Khasra (field-level plot details), and Bhu-Naksha (boundary map). All of these are now available online at upbhulekh.gov.in for free.

For residential/commercial property and builder projects: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016 (RERA) protects buyers. UP RERA was launched on October 27, 2016 at up-rera.in. Every builder project above 500 sq.m. or 8 units must be RERA-registered. Buyers can file complaints at up-rera.in for builder fraud, delay, or defects.

For all property sales: The Transfer of Property Act 1882 and the Registration Act 1908 govern how property changes hands. Every sale of immovable property above Rs. 100 must be done through a registered Sale Deed at the Sub-Registrar's office. An unregistered agreement gives no legal ownership.

For property in someone else's name (benami): The Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act 1988 (amended 2016) applies. Benami property can be confiscated by the Central Government, and the person who does benami transactions faces 1–7 years rigorous imprisonment.

For stamp duty in UP: Stamp duty is 7% of market value for men, 6% for women (on properties up to Rs. 10 lakh). For transfers among blood relatives — flat Rs. 5,000 stamp duty under the 2024 amendment. Registration fee is 1% of property value. Pay at igrsup.gov.in.

stated_source: UP Revenue Code 2006 S.30, S.31, S.32, S.221; upbhulekh.gov.in
text_to_review:
How to Check Land Records Online in UP — Khatauni, Khasra, and Bhu-Naksha

Before buying any land or taking any legal action over a land dispute, always check land records online first. This protects you from fraud and strengthens your case.

UP Bhulekh Portal (upbhulekh.gov.in) — Official government portal maintained by the Board of Revenue, UP (contact: 0522-2217145, bhulekh-up@gov.in). It is free to view. Available 24 hours.

What you can check on UP Bhulekh:
1. Real-Time Khatauni (Record of Rights) — shows registered owner's name, Khasra/plot numbers, area in hectares, tenure type (bhumidhar/asami), and revenue payable. This is legally valid and accepted by banks for loans and courts as evidence.
2. Khasra details — plot-level information including land use and survey details.
3. Dispute status — check if the plot is involved in any pending legal dispute. If yes, do NOT buy until the dispute is resolved.
4. Sale status — check if the plot has any sale restriction. A sale-restricted plot cannot be legally transferred.
5. Bhu-Naksha (boundary map) — digital cadastral map at upbhunaksha.gov.in showing exact plot boundaries. Essential for boundary disputes.

How to search:
Step 1: Visit upbhulekh.gov.in
Step 2: Click 'Khatauni (Adhikar Abhilekh) ki Nakal Dekhein'
Step 3: Select District → Tehsil → Village from dropdowns
Step 4: Search by Khasra number, Khata number, or owner name
Step 5: View and download the Real-Time Khatauni

For certified copies needed in court: Visit the Tahsildar's office and pay the prescribed fee. Online copies are valid for reference but certified copies may be required for formal court submissions.

If records show errors: File a correction application at the Tahsildar's office under Section 32 of the UP Revenue Code 2006. SDO/Tahsildar/Revenue Inspector can correct errors in Khatauni and Khasra records.

stated_source: UP Revenue Code 2006 Sections 33, 34, 35, 36
text_to_review:
Mutation (Dakhil Kharij) — Getting Land Transferred in Your Name in UP

Mutation is the process of updating the Khatauni (Record of Rights) to reflect the new owner's name after a property transfer. It is NOT the same as ownership — ownership comes from a registered Sale Deed. But mutation is essential for: applying for bank loans against the land, accessing government schemes, and as supporting evidence in disputes.

When is mutation required?
- After purchase of land by registered Sale Deed
- After inheriting land on death of the previous owner (succession mutation)
- After receiving land as a gift (registered Gift Deed required)
- After a court decree or partition order

Mutation process under UP Revenue Code 2006, Sections 33–35:
Step 1: Report the transfer to the Tahsildar of the area where the land is located — submit a written application with your registered Sale Deed / Succession Certificate / Gift Deed copy.
Step 2: The Tahsildar registers your report and issues a public proclamation inviting objections.
Step 3: If no objection is raised within the specified period and the case is undisputed, the Tahsildar directly directs the Khatauni to be updated in your name — Section 35(1)(a).
Step 4: If there is a dispute, the Tahsildar holds an inquiry, hears both parties, decides the dispute, and then updates the Khatauni accordingly.
Step 5: The Tahsildar's order can be appealed to the Sub-Divisional Officer (SDO) within 30 days — Section 35(2).

Fee: The State Government prescribes a fee for entry of mutation based on the transfer value.

Note: For property registered through the Sub-Registrar's office, the Registrar sends an automatic intimation to the Tahsildar — Section 36, UP Revenue Code 2006. But it is still advisable to separately submit the mutation application to avoid delays.

stated_source: Registration Act 1908 S.17, S.23, S.49; Transfer of Property Act 1882 S.54; UP Stamp Amendment 2024
text_to_review:
Property Registration and Stamp Duty in UP — What You Must Know

Every sale of immovable property above Rs. 100 must be registered at the Sub-Registrar's office. This is mandatory under Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908. An unregistered deed is legally invalid — Section 49 of the same Act states that an unregistered document cannot be produced as evidence in court for any right relating to immovable property.

Key rule from Supreme Court (Suraj Lamp v. State of Haryana, 2011): Power of Attorney transactions do NOT transfer ownership. Many people try to sell land through Power of Attorney to avoid stamp duty — this is illegal and the buyer gets no valid ownership.

Stamp duty rates in UP (2025):
- Male buyer: 7% of property's market value
- Female buyer: 6% of property's market value (for properties up to Rs. 10 lakh; above Rs. 10 lakh — same 7%)
- Registration fee: 1% of property value (payable separately)
- Transfer between blood relatives (sale, gift, partition): Flat Rs. 5,000 stamp duty + Rs. 1,000 processing fee — UP Stamp Amendment 2024
- Partition deed within family: Maximum Rs. 5,000 stamp duty — UP Cabinet decision September 2024

Where to pay: igrsup.gov.in — online stamp duty payment is available. You can also pay at the Sub-Registrar's office.

Registration process:
Step 1: Prepare Sale Deed with a lawyer
Step 2: Pay stamp duty (online or at bank)
Step 3: Both buyer and seller appear at Sub-Registrar's office with ID proof (Aadhaar, PAN), photographs, and fingerprints
Step 4: Sub-Registrar registers the deed and gives a registered copy
Step 5: After registration, apply for mutation at the Tahsildar's office

Deadline: Document must be presented for registration within 4 months of execution — Registration Act S.23. If missed, you can present it within a further 4 months on payment of fine, with Sub-Registrar's permission.

stated_source: UP Revenue Code 2006 S.221, S.35, S.23; RERA 2016 S.13, S.14, S.18, S.31
text_to_review:
Your Rights as a Landowner and Property Buyer in UP

As a landowner (bhumidhar) in UP:
1. Right to possess, use, and cultivate your land. Bhumidhar with transferable rights can also sell, mortgage, exchange, or gift the land.
2. Right to inspect land records free online at upbhulekh.gov.in and get certified copies from the Tahsildar — UP Revenue Code 2006, Section 221.
3. Right to mutation — to have Khatauni updated in your name after purchase or inheritance — Section 35.
4. Right against encroachment — approach SDO under Section 23; SDO must act within 3 months.
5. Right to succession — on death of a bhumidhar, land passes to legal heirs. Apply for succession mutation at Tahsildar's office.
6. Right to appeal — Tahsildar's order can be appealed to SDO (30 days), then Collector (30 days), then Commissioner (30 days), then Board of Revenue (90 days, on questions of law).

As a homebuyer (flat/plot from a builder) under RERA 2016:
1. Right to verify RERA registration before buying — check at up-rera.in.
2. Right to full information — builder must display sanctioned plans, layout, approvals, and quarterly status updates on the RERA website.
3. Right against excess advance — builder cannot take more than 10% before signing a registered Agreement for Sale — Section 13.
4. Right to the agreed flat — builder cannot change sanctioned plans without your written consent — Section 14.
5. Right to 5-year structural defect warranty — any defect reported within 5 years must be fixed free within 30 days — Section 14(3).
6. Right to possession or refund — if builder delays, you can choose: (a) stay in project + get interest for every month of delay, OR (b) withdraw and get full refund with interest from date of each payment — Section 18.
7. Right to file complaint at up-rera.in with Rs. 1,000 fee — Section 31.
8. Right to check if 70% of collected funds are in a dedicated escrow account — builder must maintain this — Section 4(2)(l)(D).

stated_source: UP Revenue Code 2006 S.23, S.227; UP Zamindari Abolition Act 1950 S.202-207
text_to_review:
Encroachment and Boundary Disputes — How to Resolve in UP

Encroachment means when someone illegally occupies or builds on your land. Boundary disputes arise when neighbors disagree on where one plot ends and another begins. Both are very common in rural UP and have specific remedies.

Step 1 — Gather your documents:
Before approaching any authority, collect: Real-Time Khatauni from upbhulekh.gov.in (showing your name as owner), Bhu-Naksha (boundary map from upbhunaksha.gov.in), and your registered Sale Deed or Succession Certificate.

Step 2 — File complaint with SDO / Tahsildar:
For boundary disputes or illegal dispossession, approach the Sub-Divisional Officer (SDO) under Section 23, UP Revenue Code 2006. The SDO will: conduct a summary inquiry, identify the rightful holder based on records, and put them in possession using force if necessary. All proceedings must be concluded within 3 months.

Step 3 — Appeal if SDO order is unfavorable:
Appeal to the Commissioner within 30 days of the SDO's order. The Commissioner's order is final at the revenue court level.

For encroachment on public/common land (village roads, chak roads, common land):
File a complaint with the Tahsildar. The encroacher is liable to a fine of Rs. 1,000–10,000 under Section 227 of the UP Revenue Code. The SDO can also issue a personal bond of up to Rs. 15,000 for future abstinence.

For destruction of boundary marks: Separate penal action available — damages payable plus criminal prosecution.

For land mafia or large-scale encroachment: File an FIR at the police station + approach the District Magistrate (DM). Also complain on CM Helpline 1076 for government intervention. In serious cases, approach the Allahabad High Court for a writ of mandamus directing action.

Do NOT take the law into your own hands: Forcibly removing an encroachment yourself can lead to a counter-case being filed against you. Follow the legal process.

stated_source: RERA 2016 S.31, S.43, S.44, S.58; UP RERA Guidelines April 2024
text_to_review:
Filing a RERA Complaint Against Your Builder in UP — Complete Guide

UP RERA (Uttar Pradesh Real Estate Regulatory Authority) handles disputes between homebuyers and builders. UP RERA handles about 40% of all RERA complaints in India, making it one of the most active authorities. Launched October 27, 2016.

Who can complain: Any person who has booked, purchased, or is in any transaction with a builder for a RERA-registered project.

Before filing: Verify the project is RERA-registered at up-rera.in. If not registered, the builder has already violated RERA Section 3 and you can complain about that too.

Step-by-step complaint process:
Step 1: Visit up-rera.in → click 'Complaints'
Step 2: A prompt asks if you want conciliation with the builder — choose 'Yes' for settlement attempt, 'No' to proceed directly to formal complaint
Step 3: Answer if there is a previous RERA order on this matter — select appropriately
Step 4: Answer if there is a pending court case — if yes, you may not be able to file RERA complaint simultaneously
Step 5: Pay Rs. 1,000 fee online — you receive a complaint number on successful payment
Step 6: Upload: allotment letter, Builder Buyer Agreement (BBA), payment receipts, and correspondence with builder
Step 7: After online filing, submit self-attested physical copies of complaint form and all documents to the UP RERA office in Lucknow or Greater Noida (NCR Bench) — mandatory as per April 2024 guidelines
Step 8: UP RERA legal division scrutinizes complaint within 7 days and communicates objections within 15 days for rectification
Step 9: After rectification, complaint is marked 'Fit for Hearing' and scheduled before a bench

What RERA can order: Possession of flat with interest for delay. Refund of entire amount with interest. Compensation for defects. Cancellation of builder's RERA registration. Penalty on builder up to 5% of project cost per day for non-compliance.

If dissatisfied with RERA order: Appeal to UP Real Estate Appellate Tribunal within 60 days. Builder must deposit at least 30% of penalty before appeal is heard — RERA S.43(5). Further appeal to Allahabad High Court within 60 days.

stated_source: Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act 1988 (amended 2016) S.2(9), S.3, S.4, S.5, S.24, S.27, S.53, S.54
text_to_review:
Benami Property — What Is It, Risks, and What Is NOT Benami

The Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act 1988, amended significantly in 2016, prohibits buying property in someone else's name to hide ownership or avoid taxes.

What is a benami transaction (Section 2(9)):
A property is benami when: (a) It is held in one person's name (benamidar) but paid for by another person (beneficial owner) for their own benefit. (b) Property is held in a fictitious name. (c) The actual owner denies knowledge of owning the property. (d) The person who paid for it cannot be traced.

Consequences of benami:
- Benami property is confiscated by the Central Government — Section 5
- The real owner LOSES all rights to recover the property — Section 4
- No compensation is paid on confiscation — Section 27(3)
- Criminal penalty: 1–7 years rigorous imprisonment + fine up to 25% of the property's fair market value — Section 53
- Providing false information: 6 months–5 years imprisonment + 10% of property value — Section 54

What is NOT benami (legal exemptions):
1. Property held by Karta (head) of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) for family benefit from known HUF sources — NOT benami.
2. Property in wife's or child's name from your declared income/known sources — NOT benami. This is a very common and legal arrangement in India.
3. Property in name of brother, sister, or lineal ancestor/descendant where both names appear as joint owners from known sources — NOT benami.
4. Trustee, executor, director, or depository holding property in fiduciary capacity — NOT benami.

How benami is enforced: An Initiating Officer (Income Tax Department) issues notice, provisionally attaches the property for 90 days, and refers the case to the Adjudicating Authority. The Adjudicating Authority then passes an order — if benami is confirmed, the property is confiscated.

For UP citizens: Report suspected benami property to the Income Tax Department (helpline: 1800-103-0025). The Initiating Officer takes action.

stated_source: UP Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act 1950; UP Revenue Code 2006 S.33
text_to_review:
Bhumidhar Rights in UP — Understanding Your Land Tenure

After the zamindari system was abolished by the UP Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act 1950, new land tenure categories were created. The most important for ordinary citizens is Bhumidhar.

What is Bhumidhar:
Bhumidhar is the highest category of land tenure in UP. A bhumidhar has permanent, heritable rights over agricultural land. There are two types:

1. Bhumidhar with Transferable Rights: Can sell, mortgage, exchange, or gift land freely. This is the most common land tenure in UP villages. Land passes to legal heirs on death.

2. Bhumidhar with Non-Transferable Rights: Cannot sell or transfer land — only inheritance is allowed. Mostly applies to land allotted under government welfare schemes. This land cannot be sold even voluntarily.

How to become a bhumidhar: Most cultivators were automatically made bhumidhar when the Act came into force in 1950. Since then, bhumidhar status passes through inheritance or legal transfer.

Bhumidhar's duties:
- Must pay land revenue (bhumi kar) to the government
- Must report transfers to the Tahsildar for mutation
- Must maintain the land and not abandon it

Inheritance of bhumidhar rights:
On death of a bhumidhar, rights pass to legal heirs. The heirs must:
1. Apply for succession mutation at the Tahsildar's office — UP Revenue Code 2006, Section 33
2. Submit death certificate of previous owner + relationship proof (legal heir certificate)
3. Tahsildar updates the Khatauni

If there is a dispute about succession:
1. Tahsildar holds a formal inquiry
2. Appeal to SDO within 30 days
3. Can proceed to civil court for title declaration if revenue remedy is inadequate

Land ceiling: Maximum land holding per family is limited under the UP Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act 1960. Excess land was acquired by the government and distributed to landless labourers.

stated_source: Transfer of Property Act 1882 S.54, S.58, S.60, S.67, S.105, S.122, S.123; Registration Act 1908 S.17
text_to_review:
How Property is Legally Transferred in India — Sale, Gift, Mortgage, and Lease

The Transfer of Property Act 1882 governs how immovable property changes hands. Understanding these modes prevents disputes.

Sale (Section 54, Transfer of Property Act 1882):
A sale is the transfer of ownership in exchange for money. For immovable property above Rs. 100: Must be done through a registered Sale Deed. The seller must deliver physical possession. Ownership transfers only on registration — NOT on payment of money alone. An agreement to sell (bayanama) does NOT transfer ownership — it is only a contract. After payment and registration, apply for mutation at the Tahsildar's office.

Gift (Section 122, 123, Transfer of Property Act 1882):
A gift is voluntary transfer without consideration (no money). For immovable property: Must be through a registered Gift Deed. Gift must be accepted by the receiver during the donor's lifetime. In UP: stamp duty of Rs. 5,000 for family gifts (2024 amendment). Gift Deed must be presented for registration within 4 months of execution.

Mortgage (Section 58, Transfer of Property Act 1882):
Mortgage is using property as security for a loan. Six types exist: simple mortgage, mortgage by deposit of title deeds (equitable — very common for bank loans, does not require registration), English mortgage, usufructuary mortgage, mortgage by conditional sale, and anomalous mortgage. After repaying the loan fully, the mortgagor has the right to get the property released — right of redemption (Section 60). If borrower defaults, lender can take legal action for foreclosure (Section 67).

Lease (Section 105, Transfer of Property Act 1882):
Lease is temporary transfer of property right for rent. Leases above 1 year must be registered. Lease of 1 year or less can be oral or written without registration.

Partition (family settlement):
When co-owners divide jointly held property. Must be through a registered Partition Deed. In UP: stamp duty on partition deeds capped at Rs. 5,000 (UP Cabinet decision, September 2024). After partition, each party applies for separate mutation.

stated_source: UP Revenue Code 2006 S.23, S.35, S.207, S.208; RERA 2016 S.44, S.58; Registration Act 1908 S.23; Benami Act S.24, S.26, S.46, S.49
text_to_review:
Time Limits and Deadlines for Property Disputes in UP

Missing a deadline in property law can permanently destroy your right to remedy. Here are the most important ones:

For Mutation:
- No strict deadline to apply for mutation, but apply within 3 months of transfer to avoid disputes
- Appeal Tahsildar's mutation order to SDO: within 30 days — UP Revenue Code 2006, Section 35(2)
- Second appeal to Board of Revenue: within 90 days from first appeal order — Section 208

For Boundary/Encroachment:
- SDO must conclude summary inquiry within 3 months of application — Section 23(3), UP Revenue Code
- Appeal SDO's order to Commissioner: within 30 days
- Commissioner's order is final at revenue level — no further appeal in revenue courts

For Property Registration:
- Must present document for registration within 4 months of execution — Registration Act 1908, Section 23
- If missed: can apply within 4 more months with SDO/District Registrar's permission and fine payment
- Documents presented after 8 months CANNOT be registered under any circumstance

For RERA Complaints:
- File RERA complaint as soon as the violation occurs — no strict limitation period but delays weaken the case

Penalties — What Builders, Encroachers, and Fraudsters Face Under Property Laws

Under RERA 2016 (for builder violations):
- Project not registered with RERA (Section 59): Fine up to 10% of project cost. Continued violation: up to 3 years imprisonment + further 10% fine, or both.
- False information given during RERA registration (Section 60): Fine up to 5% of project cost.
- Non-compliance with RERA Authority's orders (Section 63): Fine up to 5% of project cost per day of continued default — cumulative.
- Non-compliance with Appellate Tribunal's order (Section 64): Up to 3 years imprisonment + fine up to 10% of project cost, or both.
- Real estate agent operating without registration (Section 62): Rs. 10,000 per day, up to 5% of property cost.

Under UP Revenue Code 2006 (for land violations):
- Encroachment on public road, common land, or village path (Section 227): Fine Rs. 1,000–10,000 minimum. Personal bond up to Rs. 15,000 for future abstinence from encroachment.
- Destruction or removal of boundary marks: Damages payable to affected party + criminal prosecution.
- Non-compliance with SDO / Tahsildar orders: Can result in summary eviction using police force.

Under Benami Transactions Act 1988 (amended 2016):
- Entering into a benami transaction to defeat law, avoid statutory dues, or defraud creditors (Section 53): 1–7 years rigorous imprisonment + fine up to 25% of fair market value of property.
- Providing false information to Benami authorities (Section 54): 6 months–5 years rigorous imprisonment + fine up to 10% of fair market value.
- The benami property itself is confiscated — no compensation paid to the real owner.

Under Transfer of Property Act 1882 / BNS 2023:
- Fraudulent transfer of property to defeat creditors (BNS Section 320): Transfer set aside by court + criminal prosecution.
- Selling the same property to two different buyers (double sale): Criminal fraud charges + the buyer who registers first gets priority.

Under Registration Act 1908:
- Executing property documents without registration: Document becomes inadmissible in court — effectively worthless.
- Penalty for delayed registration: Fine plus interest on stamp duty shortfall.

text_to_review:
Frequently Asked Questions — Property and Land Disputes in UP

Q: I bought land 5 years ago but never got mutation done — is my ownership still valid?
A: Your ownership is valid as long as you have the registered Sale Deed from the Sub-Registrar's office. Mutation only updates the revenue record — it does not determine ownership. However, you should get mutation done immediately to avoid complications in future transactions, loans, and disputes. Apply at the Tahsildar's office with your Sale Deed copy.

Q: The person I bought land from has died — can his legal heirs claim the land back?
A: No. A registered Sale Deed is binding and transfers ownership permanently. The seller's heirs cannot reclaim land that was properly sold through a registered deed. The heirs can only inherit whatever the deceased actually owned at the time of death. Ensure you get mutation done in your name promptly.

Q: My builder promised a swimming pool and club house but is now saying the project is changed — what can I do?
A: Under RERA Section 14, the builder cannot change sanctioned plans or specifications agreed with you without your written consent. For changes to common areas (like club house, swimming pool), written consent of two-thirds of all allottees is required. File a complaint at up-rera.in demanding either delivery of promised amenities or compensation.

Q: The seller showed me a Power of Attorney (PoA) from the original owner — can I buy land based on this?
A: Be very cautious. The Supreme Court held in Suraj Lamp & Industries v. State of Haryana (2011) that Power of Attorney transactions do NOT transfer ownership of immovable property. Only a registered Sale Deed signed by the actual owner transfers ownership. If the original owner is alive, insist that they sign the Sale Deed personally. PoA-based sales are risky and have been misused extensively for fraud.

Q: Someone is farming on my land and says he has an old khatauni in his name — what should I do?
A: Get the current Real-Time Khatauni from upbhulekh.gov.in. If your name is there, file a complaint with the SDO for restoration of possession under Section 23, UP Revenue Code. If the old khatauni is from before your registered purchase, the registered Sale Deed gives you superior title. If the Khatauni shows his name, check how the dispute arose and consult a lawyer.

Q: Can I check if a plot in a new township/colony is RERA-registered before buying?
A: Yes. Visit up-rera.in and search for the project by name or developer name. If it is registered, you will see the registration number, project details, approvals, completion timeline, and any complaints filed. Never give more than 10% advance to any builder before seeing a valid RERA registration number and signing a registered Agreement for Sale.
